subtopics.title: Memory Classification, Hierarchy & Interfacing
subtopics.subtitle: RAM/ROM families, the speed-cost hierarchy, address decoding, memory- vs I/O-mapped I/O

concepts.text: Memory Classification

A microprocessor system stores programs and data in memory that the CPU reaches through three buses: the unidirectional address bus (CPU to memory), the bidirectional data bus, and the control bus (RD, WR, IO/M and similar signals). Memory is classified first by where it sits: primary (main) memory is semiconductor memory addressed directly by the CPU, while secondary storage (disk, SSD) and tertiary storage (tape) hold bulk data and are reached through I/O operations. Primary memory divides into RAM, which is volatile read/write memory, and ROM, which is non-volatile and normally read-only during operation.
Classification tree:
items: Primary memory -> RAM (volatile): SRAM, DRAM.
Primary memory -> ROM (non-volatile): mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash.
Secondary storage: hard disk (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), optical disc.
Tertiary storage: magnetic tape and other archival media.

rows: Erased by UV light through a quartz window; whole chip

concepts.text: Memory Hierarchy

No single memory is at once fast, large and cheap, so systems arrange several levels: registers -> cache (SRAM) -> main memory (DRAM) -> secondary storage (HDD/SSD) -> tertiary storage (tape). Moving down the hierarchy, each level is slower, larger and cheaper per bit. The hierarchy works because programs show locality of reference: recently used code and data (temporal locality) and their neighbours (spatial locality) are likely to be used again, so a small fast level in front of a large slow one captures most accesses.
Address Lines, Chip Capacity and Chip Count

With n address lines a device can address 2^n locations, and a chip's capacity is locations x width. An 8K x 8 chip (8 KB) has 8192 locations, so it needs 13 address lines A0 to A12 and 8 data lines; a 4K x 8 chip needs 12. To build a larger memory from smaller chips, divide: 64 KB / 8 KB = 8 chips. The chips share the data bus and the low-order address lines, and the remaining high-order lines (here A13, A14, A15, three lines for eight chips) are decoded to pick one chip at a time.

concepts.plainText: Chips = total memory / chip size = 64 KB / 8 KB = 8

concepts.text: Address Decoding and Chip Select

The CPU's address lines are split into two groups. Low-order lines go straight to the chip's address pins; high-order lines feed a decoder whose output drives the chip select (CS or CE) input, so that only one chip responds to a given address. A 74LS138 3-to-8 decoder is the standard part: three select inputs (A, B, C), three enable inputs (G1 active high, G2A and G2B active low, one of which is usually tied to IO/M so that only memory cycles enable it), and eight active-low outputs Y0 to Y7. In full (absolute) decoding every high-order line takes part, so each location has exactly one address. In partial (linear) decoding some lines are ignored to save hardware; the chip then appears at several address ranges (foldback or mirror images), which wastes address space.
Worked memory map: 64 KB on an 8085 from eight 8 KB chips.
items: A0 to A12 connect to every chip's address pins; D0 to D7 connect to every chip's data pins.
A13, A14, A15 drive the 74138 inputs A, B, C; IO/M (low for memory) enables the decoder.
Y0 (A15 A14 A13 = 000) selects chip 0: 0000H to 1FFFH.
Y4 (100): 8000H to 9FFFH; Y5 (101): A000H to BFFFH; Y6 (110): C000H to DFFFH.
Y7 (111) selects chip 7: E000H to FFFFH. Each range spans 2000H = 8192 bytes.

concepts.text: Memory-Mapped vs I/O-Mapped (Isolated) I/O

An I/O port must also be given an address. With memory-mapped I/O the port occupies a location in the memory map, so it is reached with a 16-bit address and any memory-reference instruction (on the 8085: MOV, LDA, STA, ADD M and so on) while IO/M is 0. With I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O the ports live in a separate address space reached only by IN and OUT: the 8085 uses an 8-bit port address (256 input and 256 output ports) with IO/M = 1, and the 8086 uses an 8-bit fixed address or a 16-bit address in DX (64 K ports). Memory-mapped I/O gives richer instructions but consumes memory addresses and needs more decoding; isolated I/O keeps the full 64 KB for memory and uses simpler decoding but only the accumulator can talk to a port.

Any register, direct arithmetic on port

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Memory Organisation, Decoding and Timing

A chip described as m × n has m addressable locations, each n bits wide. It needs log2(m) address pins and n data pins, plus chip select, output enable and write enable. When the required word is wider than the chip, several chips are placed side by side to form one bank (row), all sharing the same address and chip-select lines; when more words are required, banks are stacked and a decoder chooses one bank at a time. The total chip count is simply the product of these two factors.

concepts.plainText: Chips = (M / m) × (W / n) for an M × W memory built from m × n chips; decoder select lines = log2(M / m)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 32 KB (32K x 8) from 4K x 4 chips, placed at 0000H-7FFFH
Chips per bank = 8 / 4 = 2      Banks = 32K / 4K = 8      Total = 2 x 8 = 16 chips
Chip address pins: 4K = 2^12 -> A0-A11 go to every chip
Bank select: 8 banks -> 3 lines A12, A13, A14 into a 74138; enable only when A15 = 0
Bank 0: A14 A13 A12 = 000 -> 0000H-0FFFH
Bank 1: 001 -> 1000H-1FFFH   ...   Bank 7: 111 -> 7000H-7FFFH
Check: 8 banks x 1000H = 8000H bytes = 32 KB

Worked example 2: partial decoding of a 4K x 8 EPROM (A0-A11 on chip)
CS active when A15 = 0 and A14 = 1; A13 and A12 not connected
A15 A14 A13 A12   block
 0   1   0   0    4000H-4FFFH  (intended range)
 0   1   0   1    5000H-5FFFH  (image)
 0   1   1   0    6000H-6FFFH  (image)
 0   1   1   1    7000H-7FFFH  (image)
2 unused lines -> each byte answers at 2^2 = 4 addresses (1 intended + 3 images);
16 KB of address space used by a 4 KB chip

Wait states solve a speed mismatch. The processor allows a fixed time for memory to respond, set by the clock and its bus timing. If a chip is slower, external logic pulls READY low; the 8085 samples READY in T2 and inserts one wait state (Tw) of one clock period for each period READY stays low. The number of wait states is the shortfall divided by the clock period, always rounded up, because a fraction of a wait state is not possible.

concepts.plainText: Wait states = ceiling((memory access time − time allowed by CPU) / clock period)

concepts.text:
Worked example 3: wait states
Clock 5 MHz -> T = 1 / 5 MHz = 200 ns
Time allowed by CPU with no wait state: 460 ns (given)
Memory access time: 600 ns
Shortfall = 600 - 460 = 140 ns
N_w = ceil(140 / 200) = ceil(0.7) = 1 wait state
With 1 wait state the memory gets 460 + 200 = 660 ns >= 600 ns
Common mistakes in memory interfacing problems:
items: Mixing Kbit and KB: a 64 Kbit chip holds only 8 KB.
Forgetting the width factor: 1K × 4 chips need two per byte, so chip counts double.
Off-by-one on the end address: last = start + size − 1, e.g. 8000H + 1000H − 1 = 8FFFH.
Using the wrong number of chip lines: the decoded lines start just above the chip's highest address pin.
Counting images: k undecoded lines make each location answer at 2^k addresses, not k.

concepts.text: For an address range, write the decoded high-order bits, then fill the chip's own lines with all 0s for the start and all 1s for the end. For the reverse question, size = end − start + 1, and log2(size) gives the number of lines that go to the chip.

formulas.plainText: n address lines -> 2^n locations (16 lines -> 65536 = 64 KB, 20 lines -> 1 MB)
Address lines needed n = log2(locations); 8 KB = 2^13 -> 13 lines
Chip capacity in bits = locations x width; 4K x 8 = 32768 bits = 4 KB
Number of chips = total memory / chip size
8085 isolated I/O: 8-bit port address -> 256 ports (8086 with DX: 2^16 = 65536)

notes.text: 'How many address lines for 64 KB?' -> 16, because 2^16 = 65536. Work backwards with powers of two: 1 KB = 2^10 needs 10 lines, so add 1 line for every doubling (2 KB = 11, 4 KB = 12, 8 KB = 13, 16 KB = 14, 32 KB = 15, 64 KB = 16, 1 MB = 20).

Partial decoding does not make a chip bigger; it makes the same chip answer at several ranges (foldback). If a question says some address lines are 'not connected' or 'don't care', the chip's true size is fixed by the lines that reach its pins, and the mirror ranges are found by toggling the unused lines.

DRAM is denser and cheaper than SRAM because each cell is one transistor plus one capacitor, but the capacitor leaks, so a refresh cycle must rewrite every row every few milliseconds. SRAM keeps its data as long as power is present and needs no refresh, which is why cache uses SRAM and main memory uses DRAM.

formulas.title: Address lines vs memory size
formulas.plainText: n address lines -> 2^n locations (8086: 2^20 = 1 MB)
formulas.description: The width of the address bus fixes the number of addressable locations; each extra line doubles the space.

formulas.title: Chip capacity
formulas.plainText: Capacity = locations x width (e.g. 2K x 8 = 16384 bits = 2 KB)
formulas.description: A chip described as 'locations x width' stores that many bits; divide by 8 for bytes and take log2 of the locations for the address lines.

formulas.title: Number of chips
formulas.plainText: Chips = total memory / chip size; log2(chips) = decoder lines needed
formulas.description: Tells both how many identical chips build a memory and how many high-order address lines the decoder must consume (log2 of the chip count).

formulas.title: 8085 isolated I/O ports
formulas.plainText: 8085 IN/OUT use an 8-bit port address -> 256 ports
formulas.description: In I/O-mapped I/O on the 8085 the port address is one byte, giving 256 input and 256 output addresses independent of the 64 KB memory map.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between SRAM and DRAM cells?
flashcards.back: SRAM stores a bit in a flip-flop and needs no refresh; DRAM stores it as charge on a capacitor and must be refreshed every few milliseconds. DRAM is denser and cheaper, SRAM is faster.

flashcards.front: How is an EPROM erased, and how does that differ from EEPROM?
flashcards.back: EPROM is erased as a whole chip by exposing it to ultraviolet light through its quartz window. EEPROM (and flash) is erased electrically in-circuit, byte-wise for EEPROM and block-wise for flash.

flashcards.front: What happens when address decoding is partial (some high-order lines ignored)?
flashcards.back: The chip responds at more than one address range (foldback or mirror images), because the ignored lines do not affect the chip select. Hardware is cheaper but address space is wasted.

flashcards.front: Which 8085 instructions can access a port in I/O-mapped I/O, and what address size do they use?
flashcards.back: Only IN port and OUT port, with an 8-bit port address (256 ports) and IO/M = 1. In memory-mapped I/O any memory instruction (MOV, LDA, STA) can be used with a 16-bit address.

questions.questionText: A 2K x 8 memory chip in an 8085 system is selected only when A15 A14 A13 A12 A11 = 1 0 1 1 0 (full decoding). What address range does the chip occupy?
questions.explanation: 2K = 2^11 locations use A0 to A10, so A11 to A15 select the chip. The fixed pattern 10110 followed by eleven 0s is 1011 0000 0000 0000 = B000H, and with eleven 1s it is 1011 0111 1111 1111 = B7FFH.

questions.questionText: A 16K × 8 memory chip needs how many address lines?
questions.explanation: 16K = 16 × 1024 = 16384 = 2^14 locations, so n = log2(16384) = 14 address lines (A0 to A13). The 8 is the number of data lines, not address lines.

questions.questionText: A 2K × 8 static RAM has address pins, data pins, three control pins (CS, OE, WE) and two power pins (VCC, GND). What is its minimum pin count?
questions.explanation: Address pins = log2(2048) = 11, data pins = 8, so 11 + 8 + 3 + 2 = 24 pins; this is why the 6116 comes in a 24-pin package.

questions.questionText: How many 4K × 8 memory chips are needed to build 32 KB of memory for an 8-bit microprocessor?
questions.explanation: The chip is already 8 bits wide, so each bank is a single chip and chips = 32 KB / 4 KB = 8, selected one at a time by a 3-to-8 decoder.

questions.questionText: A 16K × 8 memory is to be built from 1K × 4 RAM chips. How many chips are required?
questions.explanation: Depth: 16K / 1K = 16 rows; width: 8 / 4 = 2 chips per row; total = 16 × 2 = 32. Forgetting the width factor gives 16.

questions.questionText: How many 16K × 4 chips are needed to build a 64K × 16 memory?
questions.explanation: (64K × 16) / (16K × 4) = (64/16) × (16/4) = 4 × 4 = 16 chips: four banks, each four chips wide.

questions.questionText: An 8085 system needs 4 KB of RAM built from 1K × 1 chips. How many chips are required?
questions.explanation: 4 KB = 4K × 8. Each row needs 8 one-bit chips to make a byte, and 4K / 1K = 4 rows, so 4 × 8 = 32 chips.

questions.questionText: The 2764 EPROM is a 64 Kbit device organised as 8K × 8. How many 2764 chips are needed for 32 KB of program memory?
questions.explanation: Each 2764 holds 64 Kbit / 8 = 8 KB, so 32 KB / 8 KB = 4 chips. Dividing 32 KB by 64 Kbit without converting bits to bytes gives a wrong answer.

questions.questionText: Eight 4K × 8 chips form 32 KB of memory at 0000H–7FFFH in an 8085 system. Which decoding arrangement selects the chips correctly (full decoding)?
options: A 3-to-8 decoder driven by A13, A14, A15
A 3-to-8 decoder driven by A12, A13, A14 and enabled only when A15 = 0
A 2-to-4 decoder driven by A12, A13 and enabled when A14 = 0
A 3-to-8 decoder driven by A12, A13, A14, with A15 not connected
questions.explanation: A 4K chip uses A0 to A11 (2^12 = 4096), so the next three lines A12 to A14 pick one of 8 chips, and A15 = 0 is required so the block stays in 0000H–7FFFH. Leaving A15 unconnected is partial decoding: every chip would appear again in 8000H–FFFFH. A13–A15 would suit 8K chips instead, and a 2-to-4 decoder can select only four chips.

questions.questionText: A 4K × 8 RAM in an 8085 system is selected only when A15 A14 A13 A12 = 0 1 0 1 (full decoding). Its address range is:
questions.explanation: The 4K chip uses A0 to A11. The fixed nibble 0101 followed by twelve 0s gives 5000H, and with twelve 1s gives 5FFFH. Reading the pattern in reverse bit order gives A000H.

questions.questionText: An 8K × 8 EPROM is enabled when A15 A14 A13 = 1 1 0, with all other high-order lines used by the chip itself. Its address range is:
questions.explanation: 8K = 2^13, so A0 to A12 go to the chip. 110 followed by thirteen 0s = 1100 0000 0000 0000 = C000H; with thirteen 1s = 1101 1111 1111 1111 = DFFFH.

questions.questionText: A 2K × 8 RAM begins at address 3800H. What is its last address?
questions.explanation: 2K = 2048 = 800H locations, so last = 3800H + 800H − 1 = 3FFFH. 4000H is one past the end (off-by-one), and adding 2000H treats 2K as a hex number.

questions.questionText: A memory chip occupies the address range 2000H to 27FFH with full decoding. What is its capacity?
questions.explanation: Size = 27FFH − 2000H + 1 = 800H = 2048 bytes = 2 KB.

questions.questionText: A fully decoded memory chip occupies F000H to FFFFH in an 8085 system. How many of the processor address lines connect directly to the chip's address pins?
questions.explanation: Size = FFFFH − F000H + 1 = 1000H = 4096 = 2^12, so A0 to A11 (12 lines) go to the chip and the remaining 4 lines (A15–A12 = 1111) drive the chip select.

questions.questionText: In an 8086 system (20 address lines) a 64 KB EPROM is placed at the very top of memory so that it contains the reset address FFFF0H. Its address range is:
questions.explanation: The top of a 1 MB space is FFFFFH. 64 KB = 10000H bytes, so the start is 100000H − 10000H = F0000H and the range is F0000H to FFFFFH.

questions.questionText: An 8085 memory map starts with an 8 KB ROM at 0000H, followed immediately by three 4K × 8 RAM chips placed one after another. What is the last address of the third RAM?
questions.explanation: ROM ends at 1FFFH, so RAM starts at 2000H; three 4 KB chips span 3 × 1000H = 3000H bytes, ending at 2000H + 3000H − 1 = 4FFFH.

questions.questionText: A 2K × 8 RAM uses A0–A10 and its chip select is driven by A15-bar · A14 only; A13, A12 and A11 are not connected. At how many different addresses does each RAM byte respond?
questions.explanation: Each unused line doubles the number of addresses at which a byte responds: 2^3 = 8. The chip therefore fills 4000H–7FFFH (16 KB) with eight copies of the same 2 KB.

questions.questionText: A 4K × 8 RAM uses A0–A11. Its chip select is active when A15 = 1 and A13 = 0; A14 and A12 are not decoded. Which address blocks does the RAM respond to?
questions.explanation: With A15 = 1 and A13 = 0 fixed, A14 A12 take all four values 00, 01, 10, 11, giving blocks starting at 8000H, 9000H, C000H and D000H (overall 8000H–9FFFH, C000H–DFFFH). Treating A13 as free instead of A12 gives the A000H/E000H list.

questions.questionText: A 4K × 8 EPROM (A0–A11) is selected by A15-bar · A14, with A13 and A12 left undecoded. Its first image is 4000H–4FFFH. Which of these addresses also selects the EPROM?
questions.explanation: 6ABCH = 0110 1010 1011 1100: A15 = 0 and A14 = 1, so the chip is selected (A13 A12 = 10 are ignored). 8ABCH and CABCH have A15 = 1, and 2ABCH has A14 = 0.

questions.questionText: A 74138 decoder in an 8085 system has C = A15, B = A14, A = A13 (A is the LSB input) and its enables asserted for memory cycles. Which output goes low when the CPU reads address 9A34H?
questions.explanation: 9A34H = 1001 1010 0011 0100, so A15 A14 A13 = 100 = 4, and output Y4 is selected. Taking the bits in reverse order (001) would wrongly give Y1.

questions.questionText: In an 8085 board, all memory-mapped I/O devices are selected when A15 = 1 and memory is selected only when A15 = 0. What is the maximum memory the system can have?
questions.explanation: Memory uses only addresses with A15 = 0, i.e. 0000H–7FFFH = 2^15 bytes = 32 KB; the other half of the map is given to I/O.

questions.questionText: A 64K × 1 DRAM uses address multiplexing with RAS and CAS strobes. How many address pins does the chip need?
questions.explanation: 64K = 2^16 locations need 16 address bits, sent in two halves (row, then column) over the same pins: 16 / 2 = 8 pins.

questions.questionText: A 1 Mbit memory chip is organised as 256K × 4 and does NOT multiplex its address. How many address lines does it need?
questions.explanation: Locations = 256K = 2^18, so 18 address lines. 20 lines would be right only for 1M × 1 organisation.

questions.questionText: A processor with a 100 ns clock period allows 300 ns for a memory to respond when no wait states are used, and each wait state adds one clock period. A memory with a 450 ns access time needs how many wait states?
questions.explanation: Shortfall = 450 − 300 = 150 ns; wait states = ceil(150 / 100) = ceil(1.5) = 2. One wait state gives only 400 ns, which is still too short.

questions.questionText: A cache has a hit ratio of 0.95 and an access time of 5 ns; main memory has an access time of 80 ns. Using T_eff = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m, the effective access time is:
questions.explanation: T_eff = 0.95 × 5 + 0.05 × 80 = 4.75 + 4.00 = 8.75 ns. Swapping h and (1 − h) gives 76.25 ns, and a plain average of 5 and 80 gives 42.5 ns.

questions.questionText: Cache access time is 10 ns and main memory access time is 100 ns. Using T_eff = h·t_c + (1 − h)·t_m, what hit ratio h gives an effective access time of 19 ns?
questions.explanation: 19 = 10h + 100(1 − h) = 100 − 90h, so h = 81 / 90 = 0.90. 0.81 comes from forgetting to divide by (t_m − t_c) = 90.

questions.questionText: A DRAM has 256 rows, every row must be refreshed once every 4 ms, and one row refresh takes 200 ns. What percentage of memory time is used for refresh?
questions.explanation: Refresh time per period = 256 × 200 ns = 51.2 µs; 51.2 µs / 4 ms = 0.0128 = 1.28 %. Forgetting the 256 rows gives 200 ns / 4 ms = 0.005 %, and misplacing the decimal point gives 12.8 %.

questions.questionText: A 16 KB memory for an 8085 is built from 2K × 4 chips. How many chips are needed, and how many high-order address lines must be decoded to select a bank (row) of chips?
options: 8 chips; 3 address lines to the bank decoder
16 chips; 3 address lines to the bank decoder
16 chips; 4 address lines to the bank decoder
32 chips; 4 address lines to the bank decoder
questions.explanation: Width 8 / 4 = 2 chips per bank, depth 16K / 2K = 8 banks, so 16 chips. The 2K chips use A0–A10, and 8 banks need log2(8) = 3 select lines (A11–A13).

questions.questionText: Using variable port addressing (port number in DX), how many different 8-bit I/O ports can the 8086 address?
questions.explanation: DX is a 16-bit register, so port numbers run from 0000H to FFFFH: 2^16 = 65,536 ports. 256 is the limit for the fixed 8-bit port form.

questions.questionText: In a static RAM (SRAM) cell, one bit is stored in:
options: A charged capacitor with one access transistor
A bistable latch (flip-flop) of about six transistors
questions.explanation: SRAM keeps each bit in a cross-coupled latch, so it holds data without refresh while powered. The capacitor cell is DRAM, the floating gate is EPROM/flash, and fuses are PROM.

questions.questionText: Why must dynamic RAM be refreshed periodically?
options: The charge on each cell capacitor leaks away within milliseconds
Its flip-flops lose state when the clock stops
Reading a cell sets it to all ones
Refresh is needed to erase the chip before writing
questions.explanation: A DRAM bit is charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks, so every row is read and rewritten every few milliseconds. DRAM does not use flip-flops, and refresh is not an erase operation.

questions.questionText: How is a conventional EPROM erased?
options: By applying an electrical pulse to one byte at a time
By exposing the chip to ultraviolet light through its quartz window
questions.explanation: UV light gives the trapped floating-gate electrons enough energy to escape, erasing the whole chip. Byte-wise electrical erase describes EEPROM, and fuses are used in PROM.

questions.questionText: Which of the following memories keeps its contents when power is switched off?
questions.explanation: Flash stores charge on an insulated floating gate, so it is non-volatile. SRAM, DRAM and registers are all volatile and lose their data without power.

questions.questionText: What is the main practical difference between EEPROM and flash memory?
options: EEPROM can be erased and rewritten byte by byte, while flash is erased a whole block (sector) at a time
EEPROM is volatile, while flash is non-volatile
Flash is erased by ultraviolet light, while EEPROM is erased electrically
EEPROM can be programmed only once, while flash can be reprogrammed
questions.explanation: Both are electrically erasable floating-gate memories. Block erasure makes flash denser and cheaper, which is why it is used for SSDs and firmware, while EEPROM suits small configuration data.

questions.questionText: A PROM is programmed by:
options: The manufacturer, using a mask during fabrication
The user, repeatedly, with ultraviolet erasure between programs
The user, once, by blowing selected fusible links
The CPU during normal operation, like RAM
questions.explanation: A PROM leaves the factory blank and is programmed once by the user; a blown fuse cannot be restored. Mask programming describes mask ROM and UV erasure describes EPROM.

questions.questionText: A mask ROM is best suited for:
options: Firmware that is still being developed and changed often
Very large production runs of firmware that will never change
Storing user settings that change during operation
questions.explanation: The data is fixed by a photomask at manufacture, which is cheap per chip only in large volumes and cannot be altered. Development work uses EPROM or flash, and changing settings need EEPROM.

questions.questionText: A loop body executes the same instructions again and again. Which property of programs does this illustrate, allowing a cache to be effective?
questions.explanation: Temporal locality means an item used now is likely to be used again soon, as the loop instructions are. Spatial locality refers to nearby addresses, such as the next array element.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the memory hierarchy is NOT correct?
options: Access time increases as we move from registers towards secondary storage
Capacity increases as we move from cache towards secondary storage
Cost per bit rises as we move from cache towards secondary storage
The hierarchy works because programs show locality of reference
questions.explanation: Moving down the hierarchy, each level is slower, larger and cheaper per bit, so cost per bit falls rather than rises. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing full and partial address decoding is correct?
options: Partial decoding needs fewer gates but makes each location appear at more than one address
Full decoding makes each location appear at several addresses (foldback)
Partial decoding increases the usable capacity of each memory chip
Full decoding ignores some of the high-order address lines
questions.explanation: In partial decoding some address lines are left out, which saves logic but creates mirror images and wastes address space. Full decoding uses every line so each location has a unique address, and neither scheme changes chip capacity.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of memory-mapped I/O in an 8085 system?
options: Any memory-reference instruction can be used to access a port
Data can be moved between a port and any register, not only the accumulator
Arithmetic and logic can be done directly on a port location
It leaves the complete 64 KB address space available for memory
questions.explanation: Memory-mapped ports occupy memory addresses, so they reduce the space left for memory; keeping the full 64 KB is an advantage of I/O-mapped (isolated) I/O. The other three are genuine advantages.

questions.questionText: In the 8085, during which T-state of a memory read machine cycle is the READY input first sampled to decide whether wait states are needed?
questions.explanation: The 8085 checks READY during T2. If READY is low it inserts wait states (Tw) between T2 and T3 until READY goes high, then continues with T3.

questions.questionText: In an 8085 system, which combination of signals indicates a memory read operation?
questions.explanation: IO/M low selects memory and an active-low RD means read, so together they form MEMR. IO/M = 1 with RD = 0 is an I/O read (IOR), and WR = 0 means a write.

questions.questionText: Why do DRAM chips multiplex their address pins using RAS and CAS?
options: To double the data transfer rate
To avoid the need for refresh
To halve the number of address pins, keeping the package small for large capacities
To allow the chip to be erased electrically
questions.explanation: The row address and column address are sent one after another on the same pins, latched by RAS and CAS, so a 2^16-location chip needs 8 pins instead of 16. It does not remove refresh or change the data rate.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the buses of an 8085 microprocessor system is correct?
options: The address bus is bidirectional and the data bus is unidirectional
The address bus is unidirectional (from the CPU) and the data bus is bidirectional
Both the address bus and the data bus are unidirectional
The control bus carries the data being written to memory
questions.explanation: Only the CPU places addresses on the address bus, while data travels both ways, to memory on writes and to the CPU on reads. The control bus carries timing and command signals such as RD, WR and IO/M.

questions.questionText: Which statement comparing SRAM with DRAM is NOT correct?
options: DRAM stores more bits per chip area than SRAM
SRAM costs more per bit than DRAM
SRAM must be refreshed periodically, while DRAM keeps its data without refresh
questions.explanation: It is DRAM that needs refresh, because its capacitor cells leak; SRAM latches hold data while powered. SRAM is faster but larger and dearer per bit, which is why DRAM is used for main memory.

questions.questionText: The access time of a memory chip is defined as the time from:
options: Power-on until the chip is ready for its first read
One read operation starting until the next read can start
A stable address being applied to valid data appearing at the outputs
The write strobe until the data is permanently stored
questions.explanation: Access time measures how long the chip takes to deliver data after the address is valid. The minimum time between successive starts of operations is the cycle time, which is at least as long.

questions.questionText: In a microcomputer, which memory is accessed directly by the CPU through its address bus, rather than through I/O transfers?
questions.explanation: Main memory (RAM and ROM) sits on the processor buses and is addressed directly by instructions. Disks, tapes and optical media are secondary or tertiary storage reached through I/O controllers.

subtopics.subtitle: Three programmable 8-bit ports, control word, modes 0/1/2 and BSR, 8085/8086 interfacing

concepts.text: Parallel Interface and Handshaking

A parallel interface moves a whole byte (or word) at once over eight or more data lines, so it is fast over short distances and is the natural way to connect keyboards, displays, printers, ADCs and DACs to a microprocessor. Most peripherals are far slower than the CPU, so the two sides must agree on when data is valid: this is handshaking. In simple I/O (switches, LEDs) no handshake is needed; in strobed I/O the peripheral signals 'data ready' and the port replies 'data taken', and the port can raise an interrupt so the CPU need not poll.
Typical handshake signals (active-low names carry a bar in data sheets):
items: STB (strobe): peripheral pulses it to latch input data into the port.
IBF (input buffer full): port tells the peripheral that data is latched and not yet read by the CPU.
OBF (output buffer full): port tells the peripheral that the CPU has written new data.
ACK (acknowledge): peripheral tells the port it has taken the output data.
INTR (interrupt request): port asks the CPU to service it.

concepts.text: The 8255 Programmable Peripheral Interface

The Intel 8255A is a 40-pin programmable parallel I/O chip with 24 I/O lines arranged as three 8-bit ports: Port A (PA0 to PA7), Port B (PB0 to PB7) and Port C (PC0 to PC7). Port C can be split into an upper nibble (PC7 to PC4) and a lower nibble (PC3 to PC0). Internally the ports form two groups: Group A = Port A + Port C upper, Group B = Port B + Port C lower, each with its own mode control. The CPU side has D0 to D7, RD, WR, CS, RESET and two address inputs A1 A0. A RESET puts all 24 lines into input mode 0. 'Programmable' means the direction and mode of each port are set by software, by writing a control word to the control register.
Control Word Format
I/O-mode control word (bit D7 = 1). A 1 in a direction bit means input, a 0 means output:
items: D7 = 1: selects I/O mode (D7 = 0 selects BSR mode).
D6 D5: Group A mode. 00 = mode 0, 01 = mode 1, 1x = mode 2.
D4: Port A direction (1 = input, 0 = output).
D3: Port C upper (PC7 to PC4) direction.
D2: Group B mode. 0 = mode 0, 1 = mode 1.
D1: Port B direction.
D0: Port C lower (PC3 to PC0) direction.

concepts.text: Worked calculation. Required: Port A output, Port B input, Port C upper input, Port C lower output, all in mode 0. Fill the bits: D7 = 1, D6 D5 = 00, D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 1 (C upper in), D2 = 0, D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (C lower out) -> 1000 1010 = 8AH. Two values worth memorising: 80H makes all three ports outputs in mode 0, and 9BH makes all three ports inputs in mode 0.

BSR (bit set/reset) mode. When D7 = 0 the control word does not reconfigure the ports; it sets or clears one bit of Port C. D3 D2 D1 give the bit number (000 = PC0 up to 111 = PC7) and D0 = 1 sets the bit, D0 = 0 resets it; D6 D5 D4 are don't-care and are written as 0. Setting PC3 therefore needs 0000 0111 = 07H, and resetting PC5 needs 0000 1010 = 0AH. BSR words are still written to the control register (A1 A0 = 11), not to Port C. BSR is used to pulse handshake lines and to enable the internal interrupt flip-flops (INTE) in modes 1 and 2.
Operating Modes

rows: A, B, C upper, C lower
Plain input or output, no handshake; outputs latched, inputs not latched
Input or output with handshake and optional interrupt
PC3 to PC5 handshake for A; PC0 to PC2 handshake for B
Port A carries data in both directions with handshake; B may be in mode 0 or 1
PC3 to PC7 supply STB, IBF, OBF, ACK, INTR for A
Sets or resets a single Port C bit with one control word

concepts.text: Interfacing to the 8085 and 8086

With I/O-mapped I/O on the 8085, the 8-bit port address is decoded so that address lines A1 A0 go to the 8255's A1 A0 and the remaining lines A7 to A2 (plus IO/M) generate CS. If CS is active when A7 to A2 = 100000, the four registers appear at 80H (Port A), 81H (Port B), 82H (Port C) and 83H (control). The program first writes the control word to 83H and then reads or writes the port addresses. On the 8086, whose data bus is 16 bits wide with the low byte on even addresses, the 8255 sits on the low byte and address lines A2 A1 of the 8086 feed A1 A0 of the 8255, so its registers occupy consecutive even addresses (for example 00H, 02H, 04H, 06H).

; 8085: 8255 at 80H-83H. Port A out, Port B in, PC upper in, PC lower out
        MVI  A, 8AH      ; control word 1000 1010
        OUT  83H         ; write to control register
        IN   81H         ; read switches on Port B
        OUT  80H         ; echo them to LEDs on Port A
        MVI  A, 07H      ; BSR word: set PC3
        OUT  83H         ; still goes to the control register
Typical 8255 applications:
items: Keyboard matrix: one port drives the rows, another reads the columns (scanning).
Multiplexed 7-segment display: one port sends segment data, another selects the digit.
Centronics printer: data on Port A in mode 1, STROBE and BUSY/ACK handled by Port C.
ADC/DAC interfacing: data byte on a port, start-of-conversion and end-of-conversion on Port C bits.
Stepper motor and relay drivers: sequence patterns written to an output port.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Handshake Modes, Port Addressing and Display Interfacing

In mode 1 each handshaken port borrows three Port C lines: a strobe or acknowledge input, a buffer-full output and an interrupt request. Which lines are borrowed depends on the direction, so the spare Port C lines change too. Each port also has an internal interrupt-enable flip-flop (INTE) that is not a real pin; it is set or cleared with a BSR word naming a particular Port C bit. INTR goes high only when INTE is set and the handshake says a byte is waiting to be read or the output buffer is empty.

concepts.plainText: CW = 80H + 20H (A in mode 1) + 10H (A in) + 08H (C upper in) + 04H (B in mode 1) + 02H (B in) + 01H (C lower in); mode 2 for A uses 40H instead of 20H

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: Port A mode-1 input, Port B mode-0 output,
spare PC6 and PC7 outputs, PC0-PC2 inputs
D7 = 1        I/O mode
D6 D5 = 01    Group A mode 1
D4 = 1        Port A input
D3 = 0        PC6, PC7 output (PC3-PC5 are handshake lines)
D2 = 0        Group B mode 0
D1 = 0        Port B output
D0 = 1        PC0-PC2 input
CW = 1011 0001 = B1H

Worked example 2: 8085 port addresses for an 8255
CS active when A7 A6 A5 A4 A3 A2 = 1 1 1 1 0 0; A1 A0 to the 8255
A1 A0 = 00 -> 1111 0000 = F0H  Port A
A1 A0 = 01 -> 1111 0001 = F1H  Port B
A1 A0 = 10 -> 1111 0010 = F2H  Port C
A1 A0 = 11 -> 1111 0011 = F3H  Control register
If A2 were left undecoded, F4H-F7H would select the same four registers

; 8085: 8255 at 40H-43H, common-cathode digit on Port A, driver enable on PC0
        MVI  A, 80H      ; all ports output, mode 0
        OUT  43H         ; control register
        MVI  A, 6DH      ; segments a, c, d, f, g -> digit 5
        OUT  40H         ; send pattern to Port A
        MVI  A, 01H      ; BSR word: set PC0 (digit enable)
        OUT  43H         ; BSR words also go to the control register
        HLT

The codes above assume segment a on D0 through g on D6 with the decimal point on D7, and a 1 lighting a segment. For a common-anode display the segment lights when its line is 0, so each code is complemented (digit 1 becomes F9H). A port pin cannot supply much current, so each LED or segment needs a series resistor, R = (V_supply − V_LED) / I, and often a transistor driver. Switches are read through pull-up resistors so that an open switch reads 1 and a closed one reads 0, and the program debounces them with a delay of about 10–20 ms.
Common mistakes when programming the 8255:
items: Writing a BSR word to the Port C address instead of the control register.
Using 1 for output: in the 8255 control word 1 means input.
Forgetting that D7 = 0 makes the byte a BSR word, not a mode word.
Using 80H, 81H, 82H, 83H for the four registers on an 8086 whose 8255 is wired to A2 A1; the registers are then 80H, 82H, 84H, 86H.
Assuming the ports are outputs after reset; they are all inputs until a control word is written.

concepts.text: For any control word question, write the eight bit positions D7 to D0 first, fill D7 = 1 (or 0 for BSR), then fill each field from the requirement and convert the two nibbles to hex. For a decoding question, do the reverse and check D7 before reading anything else.

formulas.plainText: 8255: 3 ports x 8 bits = 24 programmable I/O lines
I/O-mode control word: D7 = 1, D6 D5 = A mode, D4 = A dir, D3 = C upper dir, D2 = B mode, D1 = B dir, D0 = C lower dir
Mode-0 control word = 80H + 10H (A input) + 08H (C upper input) + 02H (B input) + 01H (C lower input); each flag is 1 for input, 0 for output
BSR word = 2 x bit number + S (S = 1 set, 0 reset); e.g. set PC3 -> 07H
Port A = base, Port B = base + 1, Port C = base + 2, control = base + 3 (on 8086: base, +2, +4, +6)

notes.text: Memorise 80H (all ports output, mode 0) and 9BH (all ports input, mode 0). To build any other mode-0 word, start from 80H and add 10H for Port A input, 08H for Port C upper input, 02H for Port B input and 01H for Port C lower input.

Bit D7 decides everything: D7 = 1 is an I/O-mode control word, D7 = 0 is a BSR word that touches only one Port C bit. Both are written to the control register (A1 A0 = 11), which is write-only; reading it is not allowed.

After RESET all 24 lines are inputs in mode 0, so a program must always write a control word before using the ports. In mode 1 and mode 2 the handshake lines are taken from Port C, so fewer Port C bits remain for general I/O; Port A in mode 2 uses five of them (PC3 to PC7).

formulas.title: 8255 I/O line count
formulas.plainText: 3 ports x 8 bits = 24 I/O lines
formulas.description: The 8255 provides 24 programmable I/O lines as Ports A, B and C; Port C can be split into two 4-bit halves.

formulas.title: Mode-0 control word
formulas.plainText: CW = 80H + 10H (A in) + 08H (C upper in) + 02H (B in) + 01H (C lower in); flags are 1 for input
formulas.description: Builds any mode-0 control word by adding the input-direction weights to 80H; each flag is 1 for input and 0 for output.

formulas.title: BSR control word
formulas.plainText: BSR word = 2 x bit number + S (S = 1 set, S = 0 reset), D7 = 0
formulas.description: With D7 = 0 the control word sets (S = 1) or resets (S = 0) the Port C bit whose number is in D3 D2 D1.

formulas.title: 8255 register addresses
formulas.plainText: Port A = base, Port B = base + 1, Port C = base + 2, control = base + 3
formulas.description: A1 A0 select the four internal registers, so a decoded base address gives four consecutive port addresses on the 8085 (consecutive even addresses on the 8086).

flashcards.front: What do bits D6 D5 and D2 of the 8255 I/O-mode control word select?
flashcards.back: D6 D5 select the Group A mode (00 = mode 0, 01 = mode 1, 1x = mode 2) and D2 selects the Group B mode (0 = mode 0, 1 = mode 1). D7 must be 1 for an I/O-mode word.

flashcards.front: Which 8255 control word makes all three ports inputs in mode 0, and which makes them all outputs?
flashcards.back: 9BH (1001 1011) makes Ports A, B and C inputs; 80H (1000 0000) makes them all outputs. Direction bits are 1 for input, 0 for output.

flashcards.front: How is the 8255 BSR mode selected and what does it do?
flashcards.back: A control word with D7 = 0. It sets (D0 = 1) or resets (D0 = 0) the single Port C bit numbered by D3 D2 D1, without changing the port configuration.

flashcards.front: Which 8255 mode uses handshaking, and where do the handshake signals come from?
flashcards.back: Mode 1 (strobed I/O) and mode 2 (bidirectional Port A) use handshaking; the STB, IBF, OBF, ACK and INTR signals are provided by Port C pins. Mode 0 has no handshake.

questions.questionText: An 8255 must be configured in mode 0 with Port A as input and Ports B and C as outputs. The required control word is:
questions.explanation: D7 = 1 (I/O mode), D6 D5 = 00, D4 = 1 (Port A input), D3 = 0, D2 = 0, D1 = 0, D0 = 0 gives 1001 0000 = 90H. 82H would make Port B the input, 89H makes both halves of Port C inputs.

questions.questionText: Which BSR-mode control word sets bit PC4 of the 8255 to logic 1?
questions.explanation: In BSR mode D7 = 0, D3 D2 D1 hold the bit number (100 for PC4) and D0 = 1 means set: 0000 1001 = 09H. 08H would reset PC4, and 89H has D7 = 1 so it is an I/O-mode word.

questions.questionText: In which 8255 operating mode does Port A act as a bidirectional data bus with handshaking?
questions.explanation: Mode 2 is available only for Port A and makes it an 8-bit bidirectional bus, using PC3 to PC7 for the handshake signals. Mode 0 has no handshake, mode 1 is unidirectional strobed I/O, and BSR mode only sets or resets Port C bits.

questions.questionText: An 8255 must be set to mode 0 with Port A output, Port B output, Port C upper input and Port C lower input. The control word is:
questions.explanation: D7 = 1, D6 D5 = 00, D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 1 (C upper in), D2 = 0, D1 = 0 (B out), D0 = 1 (C lower in): 1000 1001 = 89H. 92H results from taking 0 as input and 1 as output.

questions.questionText: Which mode-0 control word makes 8255 Port A an input, Port B an output, Port C upper an output and Port C lower an input?
questions.explanation: Start from 80H and add 10H for Port A input and 01H for Port C lower input: 80H + 10H + 01H = 91H (1001 0001). 93H would also make Port B an input.

questions.questionText: The control word 92H is written to an 8255. How are the ports configured?
options: Mode 0: Port A input, Port B input, Port C (both halves) output
Mode 0: Port A output, Port B output, Port C (both halves) input
Mode 0: Port A input, Port C upper input, Port B output, Port C lower output
BSR mode: bit PC1 is reset
questions.explanation: 92H = 1001 0010: D7 = 1 (I/O mode), D6 D5 = 00 and D2 = 0 (mode 0), D4 = 1 (A in), D3 = 0 (C upper out), D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (C lower out). D7 = 1 rules out BSR mode.

questions.questionText: An 8085 program writes 83H to the 8255 control register. Which configuration results?
options: Port A input, Port C upper input, Port B output, Port C lower output (all mode 0)
Port A output, Port B output, Port C input (all mode 0)
Port A output, Port C upper output, Port B input, Port C lower input (all mode 0)
Port A output in mode 1, Port B input in mode 1
questions.explanation: 83H = 1000 0011: D6 D5 = 00 and D2 = 0 give mode 0; D4 = 0 and D3 = 0 make Port A and Port C upper outputs; D1 = 1 and D0 = 1 make Port B and Port C lower inputs.

questions.questionText: Which BSR control word resets bit PC7 of an 8255 to 0?
questions.explanation: D7 = 0 (BSR), D3 D2 D1 = 111 (PC7), D0 = 0 (reset): 0000 1110 = 0EH. 0FH would set PC7, and 8EH has D7 = 1, which is an I/O-mode word.

questions.questionText: Which control word sets bit PC0 of an 8255 using the BSR mode?
questions.explanation: Bit number 000 in D3 D2 D1 and D0 = 1 (set) with D7 = 0 give 0000 0001 = 01H. 00H resets PC0, and 81H is an I/O-mode word.

questions.questionText: The byte 0BH is written to the control register of an 8255. What does it do?
options: Makes Port B an input in mode 0
questions.explanation: 0BH = 0000 1011: D7 = 0 so it is a BSR word; D3 D2 D1 = 101 = bit 5, and D0 = 1 means set. Reading D2 D1 D0 = 011 as the bit number wrongly gives PC3.

questions.questionText: PC2 of an 8255 is at 0 and must give a single positive (0 → 1 → 0) pulse using BSR mode. Which two control words, written in order to the control register, do this?
questions.explanation: Set PC2 = 2 × 2 + 1 = 05H, then reset PC2 = 2 × 2 + 0 = 04H. The reverse order gives a negative pulse, and 85H/84H have D7 = 1, so they would reconfigure the ports instead.

questions.questionText: An 8255 is programmed for Port A in mode 1 as input and Port B in mode 1 as output. The spare lines PC6 and PC7 are outputs, and unused bits are taken as 0. The control word is:
questions.explanation: D7 = 1, D6 D5 = 01 (A mode 1), D4 = 1 (A in), D3 = 0 (PC6, PC7 out), D2 = 1 (B mode 1), D1 = 0 (B out), D0 = 0 (don't care): 1011 0100 = B4H.

questions.questionText: Port A of an 8255 is used in mode 1 as an output, Port B in mode 0 as an input, the spare upper lines PC4 and PC5 as inputs, and PC0 to PC2 as outputs. The control word is:
questions.explanation: D7 = 1, D6 D5 = 01 (A mode 1), D4 = 0 (A out), D3 = 1 (PC4, PC5 in), D2 = 0 (B mode 0), D1 = 1 (B in), D0 = 0 (PC0–PC2 out): 1010 1010 = AAH. 8AH would leave Port A in mode 0.

questions.questionText: Port A of an 8255 is to work in mode 2, Port B in mode 0 as an output, and PC0 to PC2 as outputs. Taking don't-care bits as 0, the control word is:
questions.explanation: D7 = 1, D6 D5 = 10 (mode 2), D4 and D3 are don't care in mode 2 (0), D2 = 0 (B mode 0), D1 = 0 (B out), D0 = 0 (PC0–PC2 out): 1100 0000 = C0H. A0H selects mode 1, and 40H has D7 = 0.

questions.questionText: An 8255 receives the control word B6H. Which configuration does it select?
options: Port A: mode 1 input; Port B: mode 1 output
Port A: mode 2; Port B: mode 1 input
Port A: mode 1 input; Port B: mode 1 input
Port A: mode 1 output; Port B: mode 0 input
questions.explanation: B6H = 1011 0110: D6 D5 = 01 (A mode 1), D4 = 1 (A in), D3 = 0 (spare PC6, PC7 out), D2 = 1 (B mode 1), D1 = 1 (B in). Mode 2 would need D6 = 1.

questions.questionText: Port A of an 8255 is in mode 1 as an output. Its interrupt-enable flip-flop INTE A is controlled by PC6. Which BSR word enables the Port A interrupt?
questions.explanation: Enable = set PC6: D3 D2 D1 = 110, D0 = 1 gives 0000 1101 = 0DH. 09H sets PC4, which is INTE A only when Port A is a mode-1 input; 0CH resets PC6.

questions.questionText: In an 8085 system the 8255 chip select is active when A7 A6 A5 A4 A3 A2 = 0 0 1 0 0 0, and A1 A0 connect to the 8255's A1 A0. What is the address of its control register?
questions.explanation: Base = 0010 0000 = 20H (Port A), so Port B = 21H, Port C = 22H and the control register (A1 A0 = 11) = 23H. 08H and 0BH come from forgetting that the pattern sits above A1 A0.

questions.questionText: An 8255 is selected when A7 to A2 are all 1 (8085, I/O-mapped). What is the port address of Port C?
questions.explanation: Base = 1111 1100 = FCH. A1 A0 = 00, 01, 10, 11 give Port A FCH, Port B FDH, Port C FEH and the control register FFH.

questions.questionText: On an 8086, an 8255 sits on the low data byte. CPU lines A2 A1 drive the 8255's A1 A0, and CS is active when A7 to A3 = 1 0 0 0 0 and A0 = 0. What is the control register address?
questions.explanation: The registers are at even addresses: Port A = 80H, Port B = 82H, Port C = 84H, control = 86H. 83H assumes 8085-style wiring with A1 A0, and 87H is odd, which is on the high data byte.

questions.questionText: An 8255 in an 8085 system is selected whenever A7 = 1; A6 to A2 are not decoded and A1 A0 go to the chip. How many different port addresses will access Port A?
questions.explanation: Port A needs A7 = 1 and A1 A0 = 00; the five undecoded lines A6–A2 can take any value, so 2^5 = 32 addresses. 128 is the total number of addresses that select the chip, covering all four registers.

questions.questionText: A common-cathode seven-segment display is driven from an 8255 port with segment a on D0, b on D1, … g on D6 and the decimal point on D7 (a 1 lights a segment). What byte displays the digit 3?
questions.explanation: Digit 3 lights a, b, c, d, g = bits 0, 1, 2, 3, 6 = 0100 1111 = 4FH. B0H is the common-anode code, F2H reverses the bit order, and 5BH is the digit 2.

questions.questionText: A common-anode seven-segment display (a segment lights when its line is 0) is driven with a on D0 … g on D6 and the decimal point on D7 kept off. The byte for the digit 1 is:
questions.explanation: Digit 1 lights b and c; the common-cathode code is 06H, and inverting every bit for common anode gives F9H (1111 1001), with dp = 1 so it stays off. 06H is the common-cathode pattern.

questions.questionText: Eight LEDs are connected to Port B (PB0–PB7) of an 8255 with their anodes to +5 V through resistors, so an LED lights when its port bit is 0. Which byte lights only the LEDs on PB0 and PB7?
questions.explanation: PB0 and PB7 must be 0 and the rest 1: 0111 1110 = 7EH. 81H would light the other six LEDs, 7FH lights only PB7 and FEH lights only PB0.

questions.questionText: Eight switches are connected to Port A of an 8255, each with a pull-up resistor, so a closed switch reads 0. If only the switches on PA2 and PA5 are closed, IN from Port A returns:
questions.explanation: All bits are 1 except PA5 and PA2: 1101 1011 = DBH. 24H is the active-high reading (1 = closed), and BDH or 42H mark PA6 and PA1 instead of PA5 and PA2.

questions.questionText: An 8085 has an 8255 at 80H–83H configured with Port A as input and Port B as output. Port A pins carry 3CH. What does Port B output after IN 80H / CMA / OUT 81H?
questions.explanation: IN 80H loads A = 3CH; CMA forms the 1's complement, A = C3H; OUT 81H sends it to Port B. C4H would be the 2's complement (CMA does not add 1).

questions.questionText: Port A of an 8255 works in mode 2 and Port B in mode 0. How many Port C lines remain available for general-purpose I/O?
questions.explanation: Mode 2 uses PC3 to PC7 (INTRA, STBA, IBFA, ACKA, OBFA) for Port A handshaking, leaving PC0, PC1, PC2: 3 lines. 5 is the number of lines used, not left.

questions.questionText: Port A of an 8255 is a mode-1 input and Port B is in mode 1. Which Port C lines are still free for general I/O?
options: 0: all Port C lines are used
questions.explanation: Port A mode-1 input uses PC3 (INTRA), PC4 (STBA) and PC5 (IBFA); Port B mode 1 uses PC0 to PC2. That leaves PC6 and PC7, so the answer is 2: PC6 and PC7.

questions.questionText: Each 8255 occupies four consecutive port addresses. With full decoding, at most how many 8255 chips fit in the 8085's 256-address I/O space?
questions.explanation: Each chip needs 4 addresses (A1 A0), so 256 / 4 = 64 chips. 85 results from dividing by 3 ports and ignoring the control register address.

questions.questionText: An 8085 system uses three 8255 chips. How many programmable I/O lines are available in total?
questions.explanation: Each 8255 has 3 ports × 8 bits = 24 lines, so 3 × 24 = 72 lines. 9 is the number of ports.

questions.questionText: A matrix keyboard is scanned through an 8255, with 8 port lines driving the rows and 8 port lines reading the columns. How many keys can it support?
questions.explanation: Each key sits at one row–column crossing: 8 × 8 = 64 keys. 16 is only the number of port lines used.

questions.questionText: Six seven-segment digits (8 segment lines each, including the decimal point) are multiplexed from an 8255: the segment lines are shared and each digit has its own select line, with no decoder. How many port lines are needed?
questions.explanation: Shared segments use 8 lines and the digit selects use 6, so 8 + 6 = 14 lines. Driving each digit separately would need 6 × 8 = 48 lines.

questions.questionText: A four-digit multiplexed display driven by an 8255 is refreshed so that the whole display is scanned 50 times per second, each digit being lit for an equal share of each scan. How long is each digit lit per scan?
questions.explanation: One full scan takes 1 / 50 Hz = 20 ms; shared among 4 digits, each is lit for 20 / 4 = 5 ms. 20 ms is the whole scan time, not one digit's share.

questions.questionText: An LED is driven from a 5 V port output (assume 5 V when high) and needs 10 mA with a forward drop of 2 V. What series resistor is required?
questions.explanation: R = (V_supply − V_LED) / I = (5 − 2) V / 0.010 A = 300 Ω. 500 Ω ignores the LED drop, and 200 Ω uses the LED voltage alone.

questions.questionText: When an 8085 executes IN 40H, what appears on its address lines during the I/O read machine cycle?
options: 40H appears only on AD7–AD0, while A15–A8 are 00H
40H appears only on A15–A8, while AD7–AD0 carry the data from the start
The port address 40H appears on both A15–A8 and AD7–AD0
All address lines are tri-stated because I/O uses the data bus only
questions.explanation: For IN and OUT the 8085 duplicates the 8-bit port address onto the high-order and low-order address buses, so the decoder may use either half. Data follows later on AD7–AD0.

questions.questionText: On an 8086, what does IN AX, 60H do?
options: Reads port 60H into AL and port 61H into AH
Reads port 60H into both AL and AH
Reads port 60H into AH and port 61H into AL
questions.explanation: A word input reads two consecutive ports, the lower address into AL and the next into AH, matching the 8086 little-endian convention. IN always addresses I/O space, never memory.

questions.questionText: In the fixed-port form of the 8086 IN and OUT instructions (port number in the instruction), which port addresses can be used?
questions.explanation: The fixed form carries an 8-bit port number, so only ports 00H–FFH can be reached. Ports above FFH need the variable form with the address in DX.

questions.questionText: What is the state of the 8255 ports immediately after its RESET input is activated?
options: All three ports are outputs in mode 0
Port A is in mode 2 and the others are inputs
Ports keep the configuration last programmed
All three ports are inputs in mode 0
questions.explanation: RESET clears the control register and makes all 24 lines inputs in mode 0, which is the safe state for external hardware. The program must then write a new control word.

questions.questionText: With CS = 0, which 8255A operation is NOT allowed?
options: RD = 0 with A1 A0 = 11 (reading the control register)
WR = 0 with A1 A0 = 11 (writing a control word)
RD = 0 with A1 A0 = 10 (reading Port C)
WR = 0 with A1 A0 = 00 (writing Port A)
questions.explanation: The control register is write-only, so a read with A1 A0 = 11 is an illegal condition. Writing the control register and reading or writing the ports are normal operations.

questions.questionText: Group A of the 8255 consists of:
options: Port A and the lower half of Port C (PC3–PC0)
Port A and the upper half of Port C (PC7–PC4)
questions.explanation: Group A = Port A + Port C upper and Group B = Port B + Port C lower; each group has its own mode control. This is why the control word has separate direction bits for the two halves of Port C.

questions.questionText: In 8255 mode 1 input, which signal does the peripheral pulse low to load data into the Port A input latch?
questions.explanation: The peripheral asserts STB to latch its data. The 8255 answers with IBF, and INTR can then interrupt the CPU; ACK belongs to output handshaking.

questions.questionText: In 8255 mode 1 input, what does an active IBF signal tell the peripheral?
options: The CPU has written new data for the peripheral
Data has been latched into the port and the CPU has not yet read it
The peripheral must send its next byte immediately
The port is configured for bidirectional operation
questions.explanation: IBF (input buffer full) goes active after STB latches data and clears when the CPU reads the port, so the peripheral waits before sending another byte. "New data written" describes OBF.

questions.questionText: In 8255 mode 1 output, when does OBF become active (low)?
options: When the peripheral pulses ACK after taking the data
When the CPU reads the input latch
When the CPU writes a byte to the output port, telling the peripheral that data is ready
questions.explanation: OBF goes low at the end of the CPU write and goes high again when the peripheral answers with ACK. So OBF means "new data for you" and ACK means "taken".

questions.questionText: In 8255 mode 1 output, the ACK signal is:
options: Sent by the peripheral to show it has accepted the data
Sent by the 8255 to show the CPU has written data
Sent by the CPU to clear the interrupt
Generated internally to latch input data
questions.explanation: ACK (acknowledge) is an input to the 8255 driven by the peripheral after it takes the byte; it clears OBF. The 8255 itself produces OBF and INTR.

questions.questionText: Which statement about 8255 mode 0 is correct?
options: Inputs are latched by a strobe, but outputs are not latched
Outputs are latched, but inputs are not latched
Every port transfer uses a handshake on Port C
Only Port A can be used in mode 0
questions.explanation: Mode 0 is simple I/O: data written to an output port stays on its pins, while an input port simply passes the current pin levels when read. No handshake is used, and all ports and both Port C halves can be in mode 0.

questions.questionText: Which 8255 mode is NOT available for Port B?
options: Mode 0 with Port B as output
questions.explanation: Port B supports mode 0 (simple I/O) and mode 1 (strobed I/O). Mode 2, the bidirectional bus mode, exists only for Port A because it needs five Port C handshake lines.

questions.questionText: An 8255 has CS = 0, RD = 0, WR = 1, A1 = 0 and A0 = 1. What operation takes place?
options: The CPU writes the control register
questions.explanation: A1 A0 = 01 selects Port B, and RD = 0 with WR = 1 is a read. Port A would need A1 A0 = 00 and the control register 11.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the 8255 BSR mode is correct?
options: The BSR word is written to the Port C address
It sets or resets one bit of any port
It sets or resets one Port C bit without changing the configuration of Ports A, B and C
It requires D7 = 1 in the control word
questions.explanation: A BSR word has D7 = 0, is written to the control register address, and affects only the one Port C bit it names. Ports A and B cannot be bit-addressed this way.

questions.questionText: What is the main purpose of handshaking in a parallel interface?
options: To convert parallel data into serial form
To increase the number of I/O lines
To provide error correction for each byte
To synchronise data transfer between a fast CPU and a slower peripheral
questions.explanation: Handshake signals such as STB/IBF and OBF/ACK tell each side when data is valid and when it has been taken, so neither side loses or overwrites data. They do not convert, add lines or correct errors.

questions.questionText: A push-button switch read through an 8255 port gives several 0/1 changes for one press. What is the standard software remedy?
options: Read the switch as fast as possible and count every change as a press
After detecting a change, wait about 10–20 ms and read the switch again before accepting it
Program the port in mode 2 so that the switch is handshaken
Connect the switch to the control register instead of a port
questions.explanation: Mechanical contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, so a debounce delay lets them settle before the reading is accepted. Hardware debouncing with a latch or RC circuit is the other option.

subtopics.title: Serial Interface & Communication Standards
subtopics.subtitle: Async framing, synchronous blocks, baud vs bit rate, UART/8251, and RS-232, RS-422, RS-485

concepts.text: Serial vs Parallel Transmission

A serial interface sends data one bit after another over a single signal path, whereas a parallel interface sends all bits of a byte at once on separate wires. Parallel is faster over a few centimetres but needs many wires, suffers from skew and crosstalk, and becomes expensive and unreliable over distance. Serial needs only two or three wires, works over long cables and through modems or radio, and with modern signalling can be very fast; it is the choice for anything beyond the circuit board.
A link is simplex if data flows one way only (keyboard to computer, broadcast radio), half duplex if it flows both ways but only one direction at a time (walkie-talkie, two-wire RS-485), and full duplex if both directions run simultaneously (telephone, RS-232 with separate TxD and RxD lines).
Asynchronous Transmission

In asynchronous (start-stop) transmission each character is framed on its own and there is no shared clock line. The line idles at logic 1 (mark). A start bit at logic 0 (space) warns the receiver, then 5 to 8 data bits follow LSB first, an optional parity bit (even, odd or none), and 1, 1.5 or 2 stop bits at logic 1. The receiver runs its own clock, usually 16 times the baud rate, detects the falling edge of the start bit and samples each bit at its middle. Because the clocks are only nominally equal, resynchronisation happens at every start bit, so drift cannot accumulate beyond one character. Errors are reported as framing error (stop bit not 1), parity error, and overrun error (a new character arrived before the CPU read the previous one).

Worked example. At 9600 baud with the common '8N1' format (8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit) each frame carries 1 + 8 + 0 + 1 = 10 bits, so the link delivers 9600 / 10 = 960 characters per second, and each bit lasts 1/9600 = 104.2 us. Only 8 of the 10 bits are useful, so the efficiency is 80 %. With 7 data bits, even parity and 2 stop bits ('7E2') a frame is 1 + 7 + 1 + 2 = 11 bits and the same line carries only about 873 characters per second.
Synchronous Transmission

In synchronous transmission data is sent as a continuous block (frame) of many characters with no start or stop bits around each one. Transmitter and receiver share timing, either through a separate clock line or by recovering the clock from the data with a self-clocking code (Manchester, NRZI). The start of a block is marked by one or two SYN characters (16H) in character-oriented protocols such as BISYNC, or by a flag byte 01111110 in bit-oriented protocols. HDLC in one line: a bit-oriented synchronous protocol whose frame is flag, address, control, data, FCS (CRC) and flag, with bit stuffing to keep data from imitating the flag. Synchronous links have less overhead and higher throughput but need more complex hardware and cannot tolerate gaps between characters.

concepts.text: Baud rate versus bit rate. Baud rate is the number of signal changes (symbols) per second on the line; bit rate is the number of bits per second. They are equal only when each symbol carries one bit, as in ordinary two-level UART signalling. If a symbol can take M levels it carries log2(M) bits, so bit rate = baud x log2(M): a modem sending 4-level symbols at 2400 baud delivers 4800 bps. The bit time is the reciprocal of the bit rate: 1/9600 s = 104.2 us.
UART, USART and the 8251

A UART (universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter) is the hardware between a parallel CPU bus and a serial line: the transmitter loads a byte into a shift register, adds start, parity and stop bits and shifts it out at the baud rate; the receiver detects the start bit, shifts the bits in, checks parity and framing and presents the byte to the CPU. A USART also supports synchronous operation. The Intel 8251A USART is programmed after reset by writing a mode word and then a command word to its control address (C/D = 1); data is exchanged at C/D = 0 and a status word (TxRDY, RxRDY, TxEMPTY, parity, overrun and framing errors) can be read. It provides modem-control lines DTR, DSR, RTS and CTS and generates its bit timing from external TxC and RxC clocks.
8251A asynchronous mode word (written first) and command word (written next):
items: Mode D1 D0: baud-rate factor, 01 = 1x, 10 = 16x, 11 = 64x (00 would select synchronous mode).
Mode D3 D2: character length, 00 = 5, 01 = 6, 10 = 7, 11 = 8 bits.
Mode D4: parity enable; D5: 1 = even, 0 = odd parity.
Mode D7 D6: stop bits, 01 = 1, 10 = 1.5, 11 = 2.
Command bits: TxEN (transmit enable), DTR, RxE (receive enable), SBRK (send break), ER (error reset), RTS, IR (internal reset), EH (enter hunt, sync only).
Example: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, 16x clock -> mode word 0100 1110 = 4EH; enable Tx and Rx -> command word 05H (bits TxEN and RxE).

items: DB9 connector: pin 2 RxD, pin 3 TxD, pin 5 signal ground; pins 7 RTS and 8 CTS for hardware flow control; pins 4 DTR, 6 DSR, 1 DCD, 9 RI for modem control.
The voltage sense is inverted: a negative voltage is a mark (logic 1, idle), a positive voltage is a space (logic 0). The region -3 V to +3 V is undefined.

A UART works at TTL/CMOS levels (0 V and 5 V or 3.3 V), so a level converter such as the MAX232, which generates +/-10 V from a single 5 V supply with charge pumps, sits between the UART and the cable.
A null-modem cable crosses TxD and RxD (and RTS/CTS) so two DTE devices can talk directly without a modem.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Serial Timing, 8251A Programming and On-board Buses

Why the 16x clock? The receiver's clock is not locked to the transmitter, so it must find the middle of every bit on its own. When it sees the 1-to-0 edge of the start bit it counts 8 clock pulses, checks that the line is still 0 (a short noise spike would have gone back to 1), and then samples every 16 pulses, which lands close to the centre of each following bit. The two clocks may differ slightly, and the error grows bit by bit until the next start bit resets it, so the last sample (the stop bit) must still fall inside its bit cell.

concepts.plainText: Maximum total clock mismatch = 0.5 bit / (frame bits - 0.5); for a 10-bit frame 0.5/9.5 = about 5.3 %, shared between both ends

concepts.text: SPI is really two shift registers joined in a ring: on each SCLK edge the master shifts one bit out on MOSI while the slave shifts one bit out on MISO, so after eight clocks the two have swapped bytes. Clock polarity and phase (CPOL, CPHA) give four modes that master and slave must agree on. I²C instead shares two open-drain lines: the master sends START (SDA falls while SCL is high), an address byte made of the 7-bit address and a R/W bit (1 = read), and the addressed device pulls SDA low in the ninth clock as ACK. USB, by contrast, is host-polled: the host schedules every transfer, devices get a 7-bit address at enumeration, and data is NRZI coded with a 0 stuffed after six 1s.
Serial I/O on the 8085 through SID and SOD (no UART hardware):
items: SIM: accumulator D7 = SOD data, D6 = SDE (must be 1 for D7 to reach the pin); keep D3 (MSE) = 0 to leave interrupt masks unchanged.
RIM: the level on the SID pin is copied into accumulator bit D7; RAL or ANI 80H then isolates it.
A = C0H then SIM drives SOD high; A = 40H then SIM drives it low.
Each bit is held for one bit time by a delay loop: at 3 MHz and 1200 baud that is 833.3 µs, or 2500 T-states including the loop overhead.
The software must send the start bit, 8 data bits LSB first and the stop bit itself, so the CPU is busy for the whole character.

Common slips: counting a frame as 8 bits instead of start + data + parity + stop; sending or reading data MSB first; computing parity over the whole frame instead of the data bits only; forgetting the 16x or 64x factor when converting TxC to baud; treating baud and bit rate as equal for multi-level signals; and forgetting the R/W bit when forming an I²C address byte.

For any serial timing question write the frame first (e.g. 8E1 = 11 bits), then use characters/s = baud / frame bits and time = characters x frame bits / baud. For the 8251A, build the mode word right to left: factor (D1D0), length (D3D2), parity enable (D4), even/odd (D5), stop bits (D7D6).

formulas.plainText: Bit time = 1 / bit rate = 1/9600 = 104.2 us
Frame bits = 1 start + data bits + parity bit (0 or 1) + stop bits; 8N1 = 10 bits
Characters per second = baud / frame bits = 9600 / 10 = 960
Bit rate = baud x log2(M), M = number of signal levels; binary M = 2 -> bit rate = baud
Efficiency = data bits / frame bits x 100 %; 8N1 -> 8/10 = 80 %

notes.text: Throughput questions: count the frame first. 8N1 = 10 bits, 7E1 = 10 bits, 8E1 = 11 bits, 7E2 = 11 bits, then divide the baud rate by that count to get characters per second. Do not divide by 8.

RS-232 levels are inverted and bipolar: logic 1 (mark, idle) is -3 to -15 V and logic 0 (space, start bit) is +3 to +15 V. Do not confuse them with TTL levels, and remember baud rate equals bit rate only for two-level signalling.

Distance and noise immunity come from differential signalling: RS-422 and RS-485 send each bit as the difference between two wires, so common-mode noise cancels and 1200 m is reachable, while single-ended RS-232 is limited to about 15 m. RS-485 adds tri-state drivers so many nodes can share one pair (multidrop).
