flashcards.front: What are the logic levels of the start bit and stop bit in asynchronous transmission?
flashcards.back: The start bit is logic 0 (space) and the stop bit(s) are logic 1 (mark), the same level as the idle line. The receiver resynchronises on the falling edge of each start bit.

flashcards.front: How many characters per second does a 9600 baud 8N1 link deliver?
flashcards.back: 960. Each frame is 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10 bits, and 9600 / 10 = 960 characters per second (efficiency 80 %).

flashcards.front: Why can RS-485 reach 1200 m and 32 nodes when RS-232 manages only about 15 m point-to-point?
flashcards.back: RS-485 uses differential signalling on a twisted pair, so common-mode noise cancels, and tri-state drivers let many transceivers share the pair (multidrop). RS-232 is single-ended and its drivers cannot share a line.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between baud rate and bit rate?
flashcards.back: Baud rate counts symbols (signal changes) per second; bit rate counts bits per second. Bit rate = baud x log2(M), so they are equal only for two-level signalling.

questions.questionText: A 2400 baud asynchronous link uses 7 data bits, even parity and 2 stop bits. Approximately how many characters per second can it carry?
questions.explanation: Each frame has 1 start + 7 data + 1 parity + 2 stop = 11 bits, so 2400 / 11 = 218 characters per second. 300 would assume no framing overhead (2400 / 8) and 240 assumes a 10-bit frame.

questions.questionText: The duration of one bit on a 19200 bps serial line is approximately:
questions.explanation: Bit time = 1 / bit rate = 1 / 19200 = 52.08 us. 104.2 us is the bit time at 9600 bps and 26.04 us corresponds to 38400 bps.

questions.questionText: In the RS-232 standard, a logic 1 (mark) on the data line is represented by a voltage of:
questions.explanation: RS-232 uses inverted bipolar levels: logic 1 (mark, idle state) is -3 to -15 V and logic 0 (space) is +3 to +15 V. The band between -3 V and +3 V is undefined, and TTL 0/5 V levels need a converter such as the MAX232.

questions.questionText: In asynchronous serial transmission, what logic level does the line sit at while no character is being sent?
options: Alternating 1 and 0 to keep the receiver clock locked
questions.explanation: The idle line is held at mark (logic 1), so the 1-to-0 edge of the start bit can be detected. Idling at 0 would make a start bit invisible.

questions.questionText: In a standard UART frame, which bit is sent immediately after the start bit?
questions.explanation: UARTs such as the 8251A shift data out LSB first, so D0 follows the start bit; the parity bit (if any) comes after the last data bit and the stop bits close the frame.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a feature of synchronous serial transmission?
options: A clock shared by, or recovered at, the receiver
SYN characters or flag bytes marking the start of a block
Characters sent back to back with no idle gaps inside a block
A start bit and stop bit framing every character
questions.explanation: Start and stop bits around each character belong to asynchronous transmission. Synchronous links frame a whole block with SYN characters or flags and keep both ends in step with a common or recovered clock.

questions.questionText: An asynchronous frame uses 8 data bits, odd parity and 1 stop bit. How many bits does one frame contain?
questions.explanation: Frame = 1 start + 8 data + 1 parity + 1 stop = 11 bits. 10 forgets the parity bit and 9 forgets both the start bit and parity.

questions.questionText: What is the transmission efficiency (useful data bits as a percentage of frame bits) of the asynchronous format 7O1 (7 data bits, odd parity, 1 stop bit)?
questions.explanation: Frame = 1 + 7 + 1 + 1 = 10 bits, so efficiency = 7 / 10 x 100 = 70 %. 87.5 % is 7/8 (ignores framing) and 63.6 % is 7/11 (miscounts the frame as 11 bits).

questions.questionText: A 4800 baud asynchronous link uses 8 data bits, no parity and 2 stop bits (8N2). About how many characters per second can it carry?
questions.explanation: Frame = 1 + 8 + 0 + 2 = 11 bits, so 4800 / 11 = 436.4, about 436 characters/s. 480 assumes a 10-bit frame and 600 divides by 8 with no framing.

questions.questionText: A file of 14 400 bytes is sent over a 9600 baud asynchronous link using 8 data bits, even parity and 1 stop bit, with no gaps between characters. How long does the transfer take?
questions.explanation: Each byte needs 1 + 8 + 1 + 1 = 11 bits, so T = 14 400 x 11 / 9600 = 16.5 s. 12 s counts only 8 bits per byte, 15 s uses a 10-bit frame and 18 s a 12-bit frame.

questions.questionText: A modem transmits 2400 symbols per second, and each symbol can take one of 16 distinct signal states. What is its bit rate?
questions.explanation: Bit rate = baud x log2(M) = 2400 x log2(16) = 2400 x 4 = 9600 bps. 38 400 multiplies by M instead of log2(M), and 2400 assumes one bit per symbol.

questions.questionText: A channel is limited to 2400 baud, but the link must carry 9600 bps. What is the minimum number of distinct signal levels each symbol must have?
questions.explanation: Bits per symbol = 9600 / 2400 = 4, and M = 2^4 = 16 levels. 4 is the number of bits per symbol, not the number of levels.

questions.questionText: An 8251A is programmed for asynchronous operation with a 16x baud-rate factor. What receiver clock (RxC) frequency is needed for 9600 baud?
questions.explanation: RxC = factor x baud = 16 x 9600 = 153.6 kHz. 614.4 kHz would suit the 64x factor, 9.6 kHz the 1x factor, and 600 Hz divides instead of multiplying.

questions.questionText: A UART receiver uses a clock at 16 times the baud rate. After it detects the falling edge of a start bit, how many receiver clock pulses does it wait before sampling the line again to confirm a valid start bit?
questions.explanation: Waiting 8 of the 16 clocks places the sample at the middle of the start bit; if the line is still 0 the start bit is genuine, and every later bit is then sampled 16 clocks apart, at its centre.

questions.questionText: What mode word must be written to an 8251A for asynchronous operation with 8 data bits, even parity, 2 stop bits and a 16x baud-rate factor?
questions.explanation: D7D6 = 11 (2 stop), D5 = 1 (even), D4 = 1 (parity enabled), D3D2 = 11 (8 bits), D1D0 = 10 (16x) gives 1111 1110 = FEH. DEH selects odd parity, 7EH one stop bit and FFH the 64x factor.

questions.questionText: An 8251A is initialised with asynchronous mode word 7AH, and its transmit clock TxC is 76.8 kHz. How many characters per second can it send continuously?
questions.explanation: 7AH = 01 1 1 10 10: 1 stop bit, even parity enabled, 7 data bits, 16x factor. Baud = 76 800 / 16 = 4800, frame = 1 + 7 + 1 + 1 = 10 bits, so 4800 / 10 = 480 characters/s. 7680 forgets the 16x factor and 600 ignores framing.

questions.questionText: After the mode word, an 8251A receives the command word 15H. What does this command do?
options: Enables the transmitter and receiver and asserts RTS
Enables the transmitter and receiver and resets the error flags
Performs an internal reset so the next control write is a mode word
Enables only the receiver and sends a break character
questions.explanation: 15H = 0001 0101: D0 TxEN = 1, D2 RxE = 1, D4 ER (error reset) = 1; RTS (D5), IR (D6) and SBRK (D3) are all 0.

questions.questionText: An 8251A has its C/D input connected to A0. When the CPU reads from the 8251A with C/D = 1, what does it obtain?
questions.explanation: With C/D = 1 a write goes to the mode/command registers and a read returns the status word (TxRDY, RxRDY, TxEMPTY, PE, OE, FE, SYNDET, DSR). Received data is read with C/D = 0; mode and command words cannot be read back.

questions.questionText: What is the correct order for initialising an 8251A for synchronous operation after a reset?
options: Mode word, then the SYN character(s), then the command word
Command word, then mode word, then SYN character(s)
SYN character(s), then mode word, then command word
Mode word, then command word, then SYN character(s)
questions.explanation: The first control write after reset is taken as the mode word; in synchronous mode the next one or two control writes are the SYN characters, and only after that are writes interpreted as command words.

questions.questionText: Which 8251A status bit tells the CPU that a received character is waiting to be read?
questions.explanation: RxRDY goes high when a complete character has been assembled in the receive buffer. TxRDY means the transmit buffer can accept a byte and TxEMPTY means the transmitter has nothing left to send.

questions.questionText: A UART reports a framing error. What has it detected?
options: A mismatch between the received parity bit and the computed parity
A new character arriving before the CPU read the previous one
A 0 on the line at the position where a stop bit (1) was expected
The loss of the external receive clock
questions.explanation: A framing error means the stop bit was not a 1, often caused by a wrong baud rate or a break. Parity mismatch is a parity error and an unread character being overwritten is an overrun error.

questions.questionText: What causes an overrun error in a UART receiver?
options: The stop bit of a character is received as 0
The CPU fails to read a received character before the next one is fully assembled
The number of 1s in the character does not match the parity setting
The transmitter sends more stop bits than the receiver expects
questions.explanation: When a new character completes before the previous one has been read, the old one is overwritten and the overrun flag is set. The other options describe a framing error, a parity error, and a harmless condition (extra stop bits just lengthen the idle time).

questions.questionText: The 7-bit ASCII code for 'C' is 43H (100 0011₂). It is sent as an 8-bit character with even parity placed in bit 7. What is the transmitted byte?
questions.explanation: 43H has three 1s, so the even-parity bit must be 1 to make the count even; putting it in bit 7 gives 1100 0011 = C3H. 43H would be the odd-parity version, and 87H/86H put the parity in bit 0 after a shift.

questions.questionText: The byte 35H is sent in 8N1 format. Which sequence appears on the line, in order of transmission, from the start bit to the stop bit?
questions.explanation: 35H = 0011 0101; sent LSB first the data bits are 1,0,1,0,1,1,0,0, framed by a 0 start bit and a 1 stop bit: 0 10101100 1. 00110101 is the MSB-first order, and the start bit is always 0 and the stop bit 1.

questions.questionText: A receiver set for 8N1 sees the following bits after the idle line, in time order: 0 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0 1. What byte was received?
questions.explanation: Drop the start bit (0) and the stop bit (1); the data bits 1,1,0,1,0,0,1,0 arrived LSB first, so reading them from D7 down gives 0100 1011 = 4BH ('K'). D2H reads them MSB first and B4H inverts them.

questions.questionText: What is the duration of one bit on a 115 200 bps serial line?
questions.explanation: T_bit = 1 / 115 200 = 8.68 µs. 69.4 µs is the time for 8 bits and 104.2 µs is the bit time at 9600 bps.

questions.questionText: A sensor sends 500 readings per second, each reading 2 bytes, over an 8N1 asynchronous link. Choosing from the standard rates 2400, 4800, 9600 and 19 200 baud, what is the lowest rate that can keep up?
questions.explanation: Characters/s = 500 x 2 = 1000; with 10 bits per 8N1 frame the line needs 1000 x 10 = 10000 baud, so 9600 is too slow and 19 200 is the lowest adequate rate. Choosing 9600 comes from counting only 8 bits per byte (8000 bps).

questions.questionText: An RS-232 receiver input measures +1.5 V with respect to signal ground. How is this level treated by the standard?
options: It is undefined (inside the -3 V to +3 V transition region)
questions.explanation: RS-232 defines logic 0 as +3 V to +15 V and logic 1 as -3 V to -15 V; anything between -3 V and +3 V is not a valid level. A break is a space held for longer than a whole frame.

questions.questionText: What is the main job of a MAX232 chip in a microprocessor serial interface?
options: Converting parallel data to serial data
Converting between TTL/CMOS logic levels and bipolar RS-232 levels
Generating the baud-rate clock for the UART
Adding start, parity and stop bits to each character
questions.explanation: The MAX232 uses charge pumps to make about ±10 V from a 5 V supply and translates levels in both directions. Parallel-serial conversion, framing and the baud clock are handled by the UART and its clock source.

questions.questionText: On a DB9 RS-232 connector, which pin is signal ground?
questions.explanation: DB9 uses pin 5 for signal ground, pin 2 for RxD and pin 3 for TxD; pin 9 is Ring Indicator. Pin 7 is signal ground on the older DB25 connector (on DB9 it is RTS).

questions.questionText: In an RS-232 link, what are the RTS and CTS signals used for?
options: Hardware flow control (handshaking) before data is sent
Carrying the transmit and receive data
Supplying the bit clock for synchronous mode
questions.explanation: The DTE raises Request To Send and waits for Clear To Send before transmitting, which stops a slow receiver from being overrun. Data travels on TxD/RxD, and errors are flagged inside the UART, not on the cable.

questions.questionText: In RS-232 terminology, a PC serial port connected to an external modem is classed as:
options: DCE, with the modem as DTE
DTE, with the modem as DCE
DTE, and the modem is also DTE
DCE, and the modem is also DCE
questions.explanation: The computer or terminal is Data Terminal Equipment and the modem is Data Circuit-terminating (Communication) Equipment; a straight cable joins DTE to DCE, while two DTEs need a null-modem cable.

questions.questionText: Which statement about RS-485 is NOT correct?
options: Each bit is sent as the voltage difference between two wires
Many drivers and receivers (typically 32 unit loads) can share one pair
Logic 1 is sent as -3 V to -15 V measured against signal ground
It can work over roughly 1200 m of cable
questions.explanation: Single-ended ±3 V to ±15 V levels describe RS-232. RS-485 is differential, multidrop with tri-state drivers, and reaches about 1200 m at lower speeds.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT one of the SPI bus signals?
questions.explanation: SPI uses SCLK, MOSI, MISO and a slave-select (SS or CS) line per slave. SDA (serial data) belongs to the two-wire I²C bus.

questions.questionText: An SPI master talks to 5 slaves, each with its own slave-select line. How many signal lines (excluding power and ground) does the master need?
questions.explanation: SCLK, MOSI and MISO are shared, and each slave needs one SS line: 3 + 5 = 8. 4 assumes a single SS for everyone and 20 gives every slave its own four wires.

questions.questionText: Why must the SDA and SCL lines of an I²C bus have pull-up resistors?
options: The resistors set the bus clock frequency
They terminate the line to prevent reflections as in RS-485
They convert the lines to differential signalling
The devices have open-drain outputs that can only pull the line low
questions.explanation: Every I²C device can only sink current, so the line returns to 1 through the pull-up when nobody drives it. This wired-AND action allows multi-master arbitration, clock stretching and the ACK bit.

questions.questionText: How is an I²C START condition signalled?
options: SDA goes from low to high while SCL is high
SCL goes low while SDA is held high
SDA goes from high to low while SCL is high
SDA goes low while SCL is low
questions.explanation: During normal data transfer SDA may change only while SCL is low. A falling SDA while SCL is high is START, and a rising SDA while SCL is high is STOP.

questions.questionText: An I²C EEPROM has the 7-bit address 50H. What byte does the master send immediately after START to begin a read from it?
questions.explanation: The address byte is the 7-bit address shifted left one place with R/W in bit 0 (1 = read): (50H x 2) + 1 = A1H. A0H is the write address, 51H forgets the shift and 28H shifts the wrong way.

questions.questionText: On a 400 kHz I²C bus, a master sends one address byte followed by 3 data bytes, each byte acknowledged. Ignoring the START and STOP conditions, how long does this take?
questions.explanation: Each byte takes 8 data clocks + 1 ACK clock = 9 clocks, so 4 bytes = 36 clocks x 2.5 µs = 90 µs. 80 µs forgets the ACK bits, 67.5 µs forgets the address byte and 360 µs uses 100 kHz.

questions.questionText: How many devices can a single USB host controller address at most?
questions.explanation: USB device addresses are 7 bits wide (0 to 127), and address 0 is reserved for a device that has just been attached and not yet configured, leaving 127.

questions.questionText: A serial link that can carry data in both directions, but only in one direction at any given moment, is called:
questions.explanation: Half duplex shares one channel and takes turns, as on a two-wire RS-485 bus. Simplex is one way only and full duplex sends both ways at the same time.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of simplex communication?
options: An RS-232 link using separate TxD and RxD lines
Broadcast television transmission to home receivers
questions.explanation: Broadcast TV flows only from transmitter to receivers. A telephone call and an RS-232 link with separate TxD/RxD are full duplex, and two-wire RS-485 is half duplex.

questions.questionText: How is serial data normally sent and received through the SID and SOD pins of the 8085?
options: By a built-in UART that adds start and stop bits automatically
By an internal baud-rate generator driven from the CLK OUT pin
In software, one bit at a time with RIM/SIM, with bit timing produced by delay loops
By DMA transfers controlled by HOLD and HLDA
questions.explanation: The 8085 has no UART: SIM copies accumulator bit D7 to SOD and RIM copies SID into D7, so the program must build each frame bit by bit and time it with delay routines.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, which accumulator value, followed by SIM, sets the SOD pin to 1 without changing the interrupt masks?
questions.explanation: D7 is the SOD bit and D6 (SDE) must be 1 for it to be latched; D3 (MSE) = 0 leaves the masks alone, so A = 1100 0000 = C0H. 80H leaves SDE = 0, 40H outputs 0, and C8H sets MSE and would rewrite the masks.

questions.questionText: An 8085 executes RIM and the accumulator becomes 8BH (1000 1011₂). Which statement is correct?
options: SID is 0 and RST 7.5 is pending
SID is 1 and interrupts are enabled (IE = 1)
SID is 1 and RST 7.5 is masked
SID is 0 and interrupts are disabled
questions.explanation: In the RIM byte D7 = SID = 1, D6-D4 (pending 7.5, 6.5, 5.5) = 000, D3 = IE = 1, and D2-D0 = 011 means RST 7.5 unmasked with RST 6.5 and 5.5 masked.

questions.questionText: An 8085 with a 6 MHz crystal sends serial data through SOD at 1200 baud. How many T-states must elapse between successive bit outputs?
questions.explanation: The 8085 divides the crystal by 2, so the clock is 3 MHz (T = 0.333 µs). Bit time = 1/1200 = 833.3 µs, so 833.3 / 0.333 = 2500 T-states. 5000 forgets the divide-by-2.

questions.questionText: In the bit-oriented HDLC protocol, when does the transmitter insert an extra 0 into the data stream?
questions.explanation: Bit stuffing after five 1s guarantees that six 1s in a row (as in the flag 01111110) can only appear in a real flag. The receiver removes any 0 that follows five 1s.

questions.questionText: The data bits 0111111111 (a 0 followed by nine 1s) are sent in an HDLC frame. What bit sequence is transmitted for this field after bit stuffing?
questions.explanation: Count the 1s: after the fifth consecutive 1 a 0 is inserted and the count restarts, and the remaining four 1s need no stuffing, giving 01111101111. Stuffing after six 1s would give 01111110111.

questions.questionText: A 1000-byte message is sent either asynchronously in 8N1 format or synchronously as one block with 2 SYN characters and a 2-byte CRC added. How many fewer bits does the synchronous method send?
questions.explanation: Async: 1000 x 10 = 10000 bits. Sync: (1000 + 2 + 2) x 8 = 8032 bits. Saving = 1968 bits; 2000 ignores the 4 overhead bytes of the synchronous block.

subtopics.title: Direct Memory Access & DMA Controllers
subtopics.subtitle: HOLD/HLDA handshake, burst vs cycle stealing, the 8237 DMAC, DMA vs other I/O methods

concepts.text: Why DMA?

In programmed I/O the CPU moves every byte itself (IN, then MOV or STA, then a loop test) and polls a status flag while waiting, so a fast device can consume the whole processor. Interrupt-driven I/O frees the CPU while it waits, but each byte still costs an interrupt response, register saving, the service routine and a return, typically tens of clock cycles per byte. For high-speed block devices (disk, network, video, ADC sample streams) the CPU itself becomes the bottleneck. Direct Memory Access (DMA) solves this by letting a dedicated DMA controller (DMAC) transfer data directly between an I/O device and memory over the system buses, with the CPU involved only at the start and end of a block.
DMA Transfer Sequence
A block transfer proceeds in these steps:
items: 1. The CPU programs the DMAC: starting memory address, byte count, direction (read or write), transfer mode, and enables the channel.
2. The peripheral asserts DREQ (DMA request) to its channel when it has data or space.
3. The DMAC asserts HOLD (HRQ) to the CPU to request the buses.
4. The CPU completes the current machine cycle, floats (tri-states) its address, data and control buses, and replies with HLDA (hold acknowledge).

5. The DMAC now drives the buses: it asserts DACK to the device, places the address, generates IOR + MEMW (device to memory) or MEMR + IOW (memory to device), increments the address register and decrements the count register for each byte.
6. When the count reaches terminal count (TC) the DMAC asserts EOP, drops HOLD, and the CPU regains the buses; the DMAC may raise an interrupt so software knows the block is complete.

concepts.text: On the 8085 the HOLD input and HLDA output pins implement this handshake directly. The 8086 has the same HOLD/HLDA pair in minimum mode, while in maximum mode the bus is requested through the bidirectional RQ/GT lines. The essential contrast with interrupts: an interrupt (INTR to INTA) makes the CPU run a service routine, whereas a DMA request (HOLD to HLDA) makes the CPU give up the buses and stay idle or run from its prefetch queue.
DMA Transfer Modes

CPU stalled for the entire block; fastest for the device
One byte or word per HOLD, then the bus is returned and requested again
CPU slowed slightly; program progress interleaved
Transfers only in bus cycles the CPU is not using
No slowdown at all; slowest for the device; complex hardware
Where the CPU must never be stalled
Transfers continue while DREQ stays active, pause when it drops
CPU stalled only while the device keeps up

concepts.text: The Intel 8237 DMA Controller
Key features of the 8237A:
items: Four independent channels (DREQ0 to DREQ3, DACK0 to DACK3), expandable by cascading a second 8237 through one channel of the master.

Each channel has a 16-bit address register and a 16-bit word count register, so one transfer can cover up to 64 KB; a page register outside the chip supplies the upper address bits (A16 to A19) on 8086 systems.
Priority between channels is fixed (channel 0 highest, 3 lowest) or rotating, chosen in the command register.
Supports single, block and demand transfer modes plus cascade mode, in read (memory to I/O), write (I/O to memory) and verify operations, and memory-to-memory transfer using channels 0 and 1.
Auto-initialise reloads the base address and count after terminal count so a channel can repeat without CPU help; EOP signals terminal count or can be driven externally to abort.
Operates at 5 MHz in the 8237A-5 version, moving up to about 1.6 MB/s; the CPU programs it through 16 addressable registers selected by A0 to A3 while it is a bus slave.

rows: Starting address and the running address that increments or decrements each transfer
Number of transfers minus one; terminal count when it passes through zero
Transfer mode (single, block, demand, cascade), direction, auto-initialise, address increment or decrement

Mask disables a channel's DREQ; request starts a software-initiated transfer

concepts.text: Tri-stated Buses and Bus Mastership

A bus can have only one driver at a time. When the CPU acknowledges HOLD it puts its address lines, data lines and the control outputs (RD, WR, IO/M, ALE on the 8085) into the high-impedance (tri-state) condition, so they neither drive 0 nor 1 and the DMAC can take over as bus master. External address latches and bus buffers are also disabled during HLDA. Once the DMAC drops HOLD, the CPU re-enables its drivers and continues the instruction stream exactly where it left off, because no registers were altered; DMA is invisible to the running program apart from the lost bus time.
Comparison of I/O Techniques

Not involved; DREQ goes to the DMAC

concepts.text: Throughput Example

Suppose a 4 KB (4096-byte) block is to be moved from a disk controller into memory. With interrupt-driven I/O, if each byte costs about 20 us of CPU time (interrupt latency, register saving, the service routine and the return), the block occupies the CPU for 4096 x 20 us = 82 ms. With DMA in burst mode at one bus cycle of 500 ns per byte, the whole block takes 4096 x 0.5 us = 2.05 ms of bus time and no instruction execution at all; the CPU only sets up the channel (a few microseconds) and handles one completion interrupt. The DMA path is about 40 times faster here, and the ratio grows as the device gets faster.
Going Deeper: DMA Timing and Controller Programming

Bus grant is never instant. The 8085 checks HOLD once per machine cycle and gives up the bus only at the end of the cycle it is running, so the DMA latency is short, of the order of one machine cycle. HOLD is not an interrupt: DI, masks and SIM have no effect on it. After HLDA the CPU runs no bus cycles (the 8085 can only finish an internal operation already under way, and an 8086 can keep executing from its prefetch queue), and when HOLD drops it continues with no registers changed.

concepts.plainText: Fraction of bus time taken by cycle stealing = transfer rate (bytes/s) x time per stolen cycle

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: CPU load for a 20 000 byte/s device
Interrupt I/O, 25 us per byte:
  20 000 x 25 us  = 0.5 s per second  -> 50 % of the CPU
Cycle-stealing DMA, 1 us per stolen cycle:
  20 000 x 1 us   = 0.02 s per second -> 2 % of the bus
At 50 000 byte/s the interrupt method would need
  50 000 x 25 us  = 1.25 s per second -> impossible (> 100 %)
DMA at the same rate needs only 5 % of the bus.

; Worked example 2: 8237 at I/O 00H-0FH, channel 1
; 1000 bytes, I/O -> memory, from 2000H, single mode
      MVI A,00H
      OUT 0CH       ; clear byte pointer flip-flop
      OUT 02H       ; address low  = 00H
      MVI A,20H
      OUT 02H       ; address high = 20H
      MVI A,0E7H
      OUT 03H       ; count low  (999 = 03E7H)
      MVI A,03H
      OUT 03H       ; count high
      MVI A,45H
      OUT 0BH       ; mode: 01 0 0 01 01 = single, write, ch 1
      MVI A,01H
      OUT 0AH       ; clear mask bit of channel 1

Reading the example: the 16-bit registers are written through one 8-bit port, low byte first, and an internal flip-flop chooses the byte, which is why it is cleared first. The count is 1000 - 1 = 999 because terminal count occurs as the count passes from 0000H to FFFFH. The mode byte 45H is built as D7D6 = 01 (single), D5 = 0 (increment), D4 = 0 (no auto-init), D3D2 = 01 (write: I/O to memory) and D1D0 = 01 (channel 1). The block ends at 2000H + 999 = 23E7H.

Sent on data pins, latched with ADSTB
One mode; burst or cycle stealing set by DREQ timing

concepts.text: Addresses above 64 KB. The 8237 produces only A0-A15, so on an 8086 system an external page register supplies A16-A19 for each channel. The page register does not change during a transfer: if a buffer starts at 2FF00H and is 512 bytes long, the 8237 address wraps from FFFFH to 0000H after 256 bytes and the remaining data goes to 20000H, not 30000H. Drivers therefore place DMA buffers so they never cross a 64 KB boundary.
Common mistakes in DMA questions:
items: Loading the count register with N instead of N - 1 (both 8237 and 8257).
Mixing up the direction: a DMA read is memory to I/O (MEMR + IOW), a DMA write is I/O to memory (IOR + MEMW).
Confusing HLDA (CPU to DMAC) with DACK (DMAC to device).
Assuming the CPU saves registers or runs a routine during DMA; it only floats its buses.
Counting one bus cycle per byte for memory-to-memory copies; each byte needs a read and a write.

concepts.text: For DMA calculations, first find the time per byte (clocks per byte x clock period), then multiply by the number of bytes, and add any stated set-up and completion time. For the CPU fraction lost to cycle stealing, multiply the byte rate by the stolen cycle time; for interrupt I/O multiply the byte rate by the ISR time.

formulas.plainText: Burst DMA transfer time = number of bytes N x bus cycle time (4096 x 0.5 us = 2.05 ms)
Interrupt-driven CPU time = N x time per interrupt service (4096 x 20 us = 82 ms)
8237: 16-bit count register -> up to 65536 (64 KB) transfers per channel program
Maximum DMA data rate = 1 / bus cycle time (500 ns -> 2 MB/s)

notes.text: Keep the two handshakes apart: INTR -> INTA is an interrupt (the CPU runs an ISR), HOLD -> HLDA is a DMA bus request (the CPU floats its buses). The DMAC raises HOLD; the CPU answers with HLDA; the device sees DACK.

DMA bypasses the CPU, not the buses. The data still travels over the address and data buses; what changes is that the DMAC, not the CPU, generates the addresses and control signals. Also remember the 8237 word count register is loaded with (count - 1) because terminal count occurs when it decrements past zero.

Cycle stealing is named from the CPU's viewpoint: the DMAC 'steals' single bus cycles between CPU cycles, so a program slows a little but never stops. Burst mode gives the device the highest rate but stalls the CPU for the whole block, and transparent mode never stalls the CPU because it uses only cycles the CPU would have left idle.

formulas.title: Burst DMA transfer time
formulas.plainText: T_DMA = N x t_cycle
formulas.description: Time to move N bytes when the DMAC performs one transfer per bus cycle in burst mode.

formulas.title: Interrupt-driven CPU cost
formulas.plainText: T_INT = N x t_ISR (time per interrupt service)
formulas.description: CPU time consumed to move N bytes through an interrupt service routine; compare with the DMA time to see the saving.

formulas.title: 8237 maximum block size
formulas.plainText: Block max = 2^16 = 65536 bytes per channel program
formulas.description: The 16-bit address and word count registers of each 8237 channel limit a single programmed transfer to 64 KB.

formulas.plainText: R_DMA = 1 / t_cycle (bytes per second for byte-wide transfers)
formulas.description: Upper bound on DMA throughput set by the bus cycle time of the controller and memory.

flashcards.front: List the signal sequence for a DMA transfer from device request to bus release.
flashcards.back: Device asserts DREQ -> DMAC asserts HOLD -> CPU tri-states its buses and asserts HLDA -> DMAC asserts DACK and performs the transfers -> at terminal count DMAC asserts EOP and drops HOLD -> CPU resumes.

flashcards.front: How many channels does the 8237 DMAC have and how large can one transfer be?
flashcards.back: Four channels, each with a 16-bit address register and a 16-bit word count register, so a single programmed transfer can cover up to 64 KB. Two 8237s can be cascaded for more channels.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between burst mode and cycle-stealing DMA?
flashcards.back: Burst mode holds the buses until the whole block is transferred, stalling the CPU; cycle stealing takes one bus cycle per transfer and returns the bus, so the CPU keeps running with a slight slowdown.

flashcards.front: What does the CPU do with its buses when it grants a HOLD request?
flashcards.back: It finishes the current machine cycle, puts its address, data and control lines into the high-impedance (tri-state) condition and asserts HLDA, making the DMAC the bus master until HOLD is released.

questions.questionText: In which DMA mode does the controller transfer one byte, release the bus to the CPU, and then request the bus again for the next byte?
questions.explanation: Cycle stealing performs a single transfer per HOLD/HLDA handshake and returns the bus each time, so the CPU is only slightly slowed. Burst mode keeps the bus for the whole block, transparent mode uses only idle bus cycles, and cascade mode links two controllers.

questions.questionText: An 8237 DMA controller moves a 2048-byte block in burst mode, taking one bus cycle of 500 ns per byte. The total transfer time is approximately:
questions.explanation: T = N x t_cycle = 2048 x 0.5 us = 1024 us = 1.024 ms. 2.048 ms would correspond to a 1 us cycle and 0.512 ms to a 250 ns cycle.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, which output does the CPU assert to tell a DMA controller that it has released the buses?
questions.explanation: The CPU answers HOLD with Hold Acknowledge (HLDA) once its buses are floated. INTA acknowledges an interrupt, READY is an input for wait states, and DACK is sent by the DMA controller to the peripheral.

questions.questionText: Which signal does a DMA controller send to the peripheral to tell it that its DMA request is being serviced?
questions.explanation: DACK selects the device for the transfer cycle. HLDA goes from the CPU to the DMAC, DREQ goes from the device to the DMAC, and INTR is the CPU's interrupt input.

questions.questionText: How does a peripheral ask a DMA controller channel for a transfer?
options: By asserting the CPU's HOLD pin directly
By sending an interrupt to the 8259
By asserting that channel's DREQ input
By writing a command byte to the DMA controller's mode register
questions.explanation: Each DMAC channel has its own DREQ line from the device; the DMAC then raises HOLD (HRQ) to the CPU on the device's behalf. Mode register writes are done by the CPU while setting the channel up.

questions.questionText: While the 8085 is in the hold state (HLDA = 1), what is the condition of its address/data bus and its RD, WR and IO/M lines?
options: Holding the last address and data the CPU placed on them
questions.explanation: In the hold state the CPU floats its bus drivers so the DMAC can drive them as bus master; two drivers on one line would clash.

questions.questionText: What is the correct order of signals in a DMA transfer request?
questions.explanation: The device raises DREQ, the DMAC requests the bus with HOLD, the CPU grants it with HLDA, and only then does the DMAC acknowledge the device with DACK and run the transfer.

questions.questionText: Which statement about DMA is NOT correct?
options: The CPU pushes its registers onto the stack before the DMA transfer begins
The data still travels over the system address and data buses
The DMA controller generates the memory addresses and read/write strobes
The CPU must program the DMA controller before the transfer starts
questions.explanation: No registers are saved because the CPU runs no service routine; it just floats its buses and resumes exactly where it stopped. The other three statements are true.

questions.questionText: What is the main drawback of programmed (polled) I/O for a fast device?
options: It needs an extra DMA controller chip
It requires a separate interrupt controller
The CPU wastes time repeatedly testing a status flag and moving every byte itself
It cannot transfer data from memory to an output port
questions.explanation: In programmed I/O the processor loops on the status bit and executes the IN/OUT and memory instructions for every byte, so little time is left for other work. It needs no extra hardware at all.

questions.questionText: An 8085 has just executed DI (disable interrupts). A DMA controller now raises HOLD. What happens?
options: The request is ignored until an EI instruction is executed
The CPU releases the buses at once, even in the middle of a machine cycle
The CPU treats HOLD as a TRAP and jumps to 0024H
The CPU finishes its current machine cycle, floats its buses and asserts HLDA
questions.explanation: HOLD is a bus request, not an interrupt, so DI and the interrupt masks have no effect on it. The 8085 grants the bus only at the end of the current machine cycle.

questions.questionText: How does a bus master request the buses from an 8086 operating in maximum mode?
options: Through the HOLD input and HLDA output
Through the bidirectional RQ/GT0 or RQ/GT1 pins
questions.explanation: In maximum mode the HOLD/HLDA pins are reused, and bus requests use the request/grant pins: a pulse from the master requests, a pulse from the 8086 grants, and a pulse from the master releases. HOLD/HLDA are used in minimum mode.

questions.questionText: Which DMA mode transfers data only during bus cycles that the CPU is not using, so the program is never slowed down?
questions.explanation: Transparent DMA fits transfers into idle bus time, such as internal decode or execute cycles, giving zero CPU slowdown at the cost of the slowest device rate and extra logic to detect free cycles.

questions.questionText: Which DMA mode gives a peripheral the highest transfer rate but keeps the CPU off the bus for the entire block?
questions.explanation: In burst mode the DMAC holds the bus until the whole block (or terminal count) is done, so transfers run back to back while the CPU waits.

questions.questionText: In the 8237 demand transfer mode, how long does the channel keep transferring?
options: For exactly one byte per DREQ, then the bus is always returned
Until terminal count, regardless of the DREQ level
As long as DREQ stays active, pausing when DREQ goes inactive and resuming when it returns
Only during bus cycles the CPU leaves idle
questions.explanation: Demand mode lets the device control the flow: it transfers while DREQ is held and releases the bus when the device runs out of data, until TC or EOP ends the block. The other options describe single, block and transparent operation.

questions.questionText: How many independent DMA channels does a single Intel 8237A provide?
questions.explanation: The 8237A has four channels (DREQ0-3/DACK0-3). More are obtained by cascading further 8237s into its channels.

questions.questionText: An 8237 channel is to transfer a block of 512 bytes. What value must be loaded into its base word count register?
questions.explanation: The count is loaded with N - 1 because terminal count occurs when the register decrements past 0000H: 512 - 1 = 511 = 01FFH. 0200H is 512 itself and 0512H writes the decimal digits as hex.

questions.questionText: An 8237 channel is programmed with base address 3000H, word count 00FFH and address increment. How many bytes are transferred, and what is the address of the last byte?
questions.explanation: Transfers = count + 1 = 00FFH + 1 = 256. Addresses run 3000H to 3000H + 00FFH = 30FFH. 3100H would be one byte beyond the block.

questions.questionText: What 8237 mode register byte selects channel 2, block transfer, read transfer (memory to I/O), address increment and auto-initialisation?
questions.explanation: D7D6 = 10 (block), D5 = 0 (increment), D4 = 1 (auto-init), D3D2 = 10 (read), D1D0 = 10 (channel 2): 1001 1010 = 9AH. 96H selects a write transfer, 8AH omits auto-init and 5AH is single mode.

questions.questionText: The byte 48H is written to the 8237 mode register. How is the channel configured?
options: Channel 0, single transfer, read (memory to I/O), address increment, no auto-initialise
Channel 2, single transfer, read (memory to I/O), address increment, no auto-initialise
Channel 0, block transfer, write (I/O to memory), address increment, no auto-initialise
Channel 0, single transfer, write (I/O to memory), address decrement, auto-initialise
questions.explanation: 48H = 01 0 0 10 00: D7D6 = 01 single mode, D5 = 0 increment, D4 = 0 no auto-init, D3D2 = 10 read transfer, D1D0 = 00 channel 0.

questions.questionText: In 8237 terminology, what does a 'read transfer' do?
options: Moves data from an I/O device to memory (IOR and MEMW active)
Reads the channel's status register into the CPU
Moves data from memory to an I/O device (MEMR and IOW active)
Checks addresses without any data being moved
questions.explanation: DMA read and write are named from memory's point of view: a read transfer reads memory and writes it to the device. I/O to memory is a write transfer, and address-only cycles are verify transfers.

questions.questionText: Which 8237 transfer type generates addresses and counts down like a normal transfer but activates no memory or I/O read/write strobes?
questions.explanation: A verify transfer runs the address and count machinery without moving data, which is useful for testing a channel or for devices that check data themselves. Cascade is a mode for linking controllers, not a transfer type.

questions.questionText: Which 8237 channels are used for a memory-to-memory transfer?
options: Any two channels chosen in the mode register
questions.explanation: Channel 0 supplies the source address and channel 1 the destination address and count; each byte is read into the 8237's temporary register and then written out. Memory-to-memory is enabled in the command register.

questions.questionText: What does auto-initialisation do on an 8237 channel?
options: Clears all channel registers when the chip is reset
Automatically unmasks all four channels at power-on
Reloads the current address and count registers from the base registers after terminal count
Programs the mode register with a default value
questions.explanation: The base registers keep the original start address and count, and with auto-init set the channel copies them back at TC so it can repeat the same buffer with no CPU help.

questions.questionText: Which description of the 8237 EOP pin is correct?
options: It is an input only, used to request a DMA cycle
It is bidirectional: the 8237 drives it low at terminal count, and an external low input ends the transfer
It is an output that requests the bus from the CPU
It is an output that strobes the upper address byte into a latch
questions.explanation: End Of Process signals completion and also lets hardware abort a transfer early. Bus requests use HRQ, and the upper-address strobe is ADSTB.

questions.questionText: One master 8237 has all four of its channels in cascade mode, each connected to a slave 8237. How many DMA channels are available to peripherals?
questions.explanation: A master channel in cascade mode only passes on the slave's HRQ/HLDA handshake and does no transfers itself, so the usable channels are 4 slaves x 4 = 16. 20 wrongly counts the master's four channels as well.

questions.questionText: An 8237 uses fixed priority. DREQ1 and DREQ3 become active at exactly the same time. Which channel is serviced first?
questions.explanation: In fixed priority channel 0 is highest and channel 3 lowest, so channel 1 wins. Serving the least recently used channel describes rotating priority.

questions.questionText: An 8237 is set for rotating priority, and channel 1 has just been serviced. Which channel now has the highest priority?
questions.explanation: With rotating priority the channel just served drops to the lowest level, so the order becomes 2, 3, 0, 1 and channel 2 is highest.

questions.questionText: In an 8086-based PC, a DMA channel has page register 2H and 8237 address FF00H, and is programmed to transfer 512 bytes with address increment. Where do the bytes go?
options: All 512 go to 2FF00H-300FFH, because the page register increments automatically
Only 256 bytes are moved and then terminal count is reached
The first 256 go to 2FF00H-2FFFFH; the rest wrap to 20000H-200FFH
The first 256 go to 2FF00H-2FFFFH; the rest go to 1FF00H-1FFFFH
questions.explanation: The 8237 address counter is only 16 bits: after FFFFH it wraps to 0000H, and the external page register does not change, so bytes 257-512 land at 20000H-200FFH. Buffers must therefore not cross a 64 KB page boundary.

questions.questionText: In a PC, a DMA page register holds 0AH and the 8237 channel's current address is 3400H. What 20-bit physical address is placed on the bus?
questions.explanation: The page register supplies A19-A16 and the 8237 supplies A15-A0, so the address is 0AH followed by 3400H = A3400H. Adding the page x 16 as if it were a segment gives 034A0H.

questions.questionText: A DMA controller in burst mode needs one 250 ns bus cycle per byte. What is its maximum transfer rate?
questions.explanation: Rate = 1 / t_cycle = 1 / 250 ns = 4 x 10^6 bytes/s = 4 MB/s. 2 MB/s corresponds to a 500 ns cycle.

questions.questionText: A device delivers 20 000 bytes/s. With interrupt-driven I/O each byte costs 30 µs of CPU time; with cycle-stealing DMA each byte steals one 0.5 µs bus cycle from the CPU. What percentage of the CPU's time is freed by switching to DMA?
questions.explanation: Interrupt I/O uses 20 000 x 30 µs = 0.6 s per second = 60 %; DMA steals 20 000 x 0.5 µs = 0.01 s = 1 %. Time freed = 60 - 1 = 59 %. 60 % ignores the cycles DMA still steals.

questions.questionText: A disk controller uses cycle-stealing DMA at 50 000 bytes/s, and each stolen bus cycle lasts 400 ns. What fraction of the bus time is taken from the CPU?
questions.explanation: Fraction = rate x t_cycle = 50 000 x 400 ns = 0.02 = 2 % of every second. 20 % and 0.2 % are power-of-ten slips in the unit conversion.

questions.questionText: A DMA controller clocked at 5 MHz needs 4 clock cycles per byte in burst mode. Setting up the channel and handling the completion interrupt cost the CPU a further 20 µs. What is the total time to move an 8 KB (8192-byte) block?
questions.explanation: One byte = 4 x 0.2 µs = 0.8 µs, so the block takes 8192 x 0.8 µs = 6553.6 µs, and adding 20 µs gives 6573.6 µs = 6.57 ms. 1.66 ms uses one clock per byte and 32.79 ms treats the clock period as 1 µs.

questions.questionText: A 4 KB (4096-byte) block can be moved either by interrupt-driven I/O at 16 µs of CPU time per byte, or by burst DMA at 0.4 µs per byte plus 50 µs for set-up and completion. To the nearest whole number, by what factor is DMA faster?
questions.explanation: Interrupt: 4096 x 16 µs = 65536 µs. DMA: 4096 x 0.4 + 50 = 1688.4 µs. Ratio = 65536 / 1688.4 = 38.8, which rounds to 39. 40 ignores the 50 µs overhead (16 / 0.4).

questions.questionText: The 8257's terminal count register uses 14 bits for the byte count. What is the largest block one 8257 channel can transfer before it must be reprogrammed?
questions.explanation: 14 bits hold N - 1 from 0 to 16 383, so N can be up to 2^14 = 16384 bytes. 64 KB is the 8237's limit with its 16-bit count, and 16 383 is the largest value in the register, not the block size.

questions.questionText: An 8257 channel must perform a DMA read (memory to I/O) of 100 bytes. What 16-bit value is written to its terminal count register?
questions.explanation: Bits 15-14 select the operation (10 = read, 01 = write, 00 = verify) and bits 13-0 hold N - 1 = 99 = 0063H, giving 8063H. 4063H selects a write, 8064H loads N instead of N - 1, and 0063H has no operation bits.

questions.questionText: During an 8257 DMA cycle, how are address lines A8-A15 supplied to the system bus?
options: They come from a dedicated set of eight address pins on the 8257
They are output on the 8257's data pins and latched by an external latch (such as the 8212) using ADSTB
The CPU keeps driving them while in the hold state
They are fixed at 00H, so the 8257 can only reach the first 256 bytes
questions.explanation: The 8257 drives A0-A7 directly but multiplexes the upper address byte onto D0-D7, and ADSTB strobes it into an 8212; AEN keeps other bus drivers off during DMA.

questions.questionText: What does the auto load feature of the 8257 do?
options: At terminal count, it reloads every channel from its own base registers
It loads the mode set register automatically after reset
It lets channel 0 and channel 1 perform memory-to-memory copies
At terminal count, it reloads channel 2's address and count from channel 3's registers
questions.explanation: In auto load mode channel 3 holds the reload parameters for channel 2, so repeated or chained blocks can run without CPU intervention. Per-channel base registers are an 8237 feature, and the 8257 has no memory-to-memory mode.

questions.questionText: While the CPU is writing the address, count and mode registers of an 8237, the 8237 is acting as:
options: A slave I/O device selected by CS and addressed by A0-A3
A memory device mapped at address 0000H
questions.explanation: The DMAC has two roles: it is a programmable slave during set-up (in its idle state) and becomes the bus master only after it receives HLDA.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly contrasts interrupt-driven I/O with DMA?
options: In interrupt I/O the CPU runs a service routine for each transfer; in DMA the controller moves the data and the CPU is involved only at the start and end of the block
In both methods the CPU executes an instruction for every byte transferred
Interrupt I/O needs a HOLD/HLDA handshake, while DMA needs INTR/INTA
DMA is preferred for slow, occasional devices such as keyboards
questions.explanation: Interrupt I/O removes busy waiting but still costs an ISR per byte, whereas DMA removes the CPU from the data path. The handshakes are the other way round, and DMA suits fast block devices.

questions.questionText: Which Intel chip is a programmable DMA controller?
questions.explanation: The 8237 (and the earlier 8257) are DMA controllers. The 8259 is an interrupt controller, the 8255 a parallel interface and the 8251 a USART.

questions.questionText: On the 8085, what kind of pin is HLDA?
options: An open-drain input shared with READY
questions.explanation: HOLD is an input that receives the bus request and HLDA is an output that grants it. Bidirectional request/grant pins exist only on the 8086 in maximum mode.

questions.questionText: How many bus cycles does an 8237 need to copy a 1000-byte block from one memory area to another using its memory-to-memory mode?
questions.explanation: Each byte needs a memory read into the temporary register and then a memory write, so 2 x 1000 = 2000 bus cycles. 1000 assumes a single cycle per byte as in memory-I/O transfers.

questions.questionText: While an 8086 is in the hold state, what can it still do?
options: Fetch new instruction bytes from memory
Respond to an INTR by reading the interrupt vector
Write the results of instructions to memory
Execute instructions already in its prefetch queue that need no bus cycles
questions.explanation: The BIU has given up the bus, so any fetch, memory access or interrupt acknowledge must wait; the EU can keep running from the queue until it needs the bus.

questions.questionText: What does terminal count (TC) indicate on a DMA controller channel?
options: The channel has been given the highest priority
The programmed number of transfers has been completed
The CPU has granted the buses
questions.explanation: TC is reached when the word count runs out; the DMAC then signals it (EOP on the 8237, TC pin on the 8257) and the block is finished.

questions.questionText: During a DMA transfer, which device generates the memory address on the address bus?
questions.explanation: Once it holds the bus the DMAC outputs the address from its current address register and increments or decrements it after each transfer.

questions.questionText: The CPU reads the 8237 status register and gets 21H. What does this mean?
options: Channel 1 has reached terminal count and channel 0 has a pending request
Channels 0 and 5 have reached terminal count
Channel 0 has reached terminal count and channel 1 has a pending DMA request
Channel 2 has reached terminal count and channel 1 is masked
questions.explanation: Bits D3-D0 flag terminal count for channels 3-0 and bits D7-D4 flag pending requests. 21H = 0010 0001: D0 = 1 (TC on channel 0) and D5 = 1 (request on channel 1).

questions.questionText: The byte 05H is written to the 8237 single mask register. What is the effect?
options: The mask bit of channel 1 is cleared, so channel 1 is enabled
The mask bits of channels 0 and 2 are set
Channel 5 is masked in the slave controller
The mask bit of channel 1 is set, so DREQ1 is ignored
questions.explanation: In the single mask register D1D0 select the channel and D2 = 1 sets (D2 = 0 clears) its mask bit. 05H = 0000 0101: D2 = 1 and D1D0 = 01, so channel 1 is masked.
